At the monthly rate that is $1,548 a year taken on trust, and the two figures the site leads with are its own: a “$20k to $80k a month” mission at a named store, and “~$38,000 in annual profit leakage identified for one connected business”. To its credit the site labels the first a goal in progress rather than a result, and says plainly that the SOC 2 Type II and ISO/IEC 27001 certifications on its security page belong to Supabase and AWS rather than to GrowGiant. That is more candour than this category usually offers. It is still not evidence.

One last tension worth naming. The product is sold as “The AI Chief Executive Officer that guides planning and execution across your entire business”, and clause 7 of its own terms states that AI can be wrong and that reviewing the output before you rely on it for business, financial, legal or tax decisions is your job. Both statements are fair. They describe very different products, and the second one is the contract.

HelpCenter is genuinely best for small Shopify stores that want ticketing, live chat and a searchable FAQ page from one app rather than bolting three together. Skip it if you already run a general helpdesk like Zendesk or Freshdesk for a business wider than the store — this is Shopify-shaped, not company-shaped.

(re-read 2026-08-29 on apps.shopify.com/helpcenter) Free to install, and the meter is tickets rather than agents — Basic already gives unlimited support agents, then bills for every ticket over the allowance. Free covers 10 tickets a month and charges $0.25 for each one after that. Basic is $5.99 a month or $59.99 a year, a 17% saving, and covers 50 tickets, then $0.16 each. Standard is $19.99 or $199.99 a year for 300 tickets, then $0.15. Advanced is $49.99 or $498.96 a year for 1,000 tickets, then $0.10. Every paid tier carries a 14-day free trial and all charges are billed in USD. Which means the headline $5.99 only holds to 50 tickets a month: at 300 tickets Basic works out at $45.99, because the 250 over the allowance add $40 — while Standard includes those same 300 for $19.99. Price the tier against your own ticket count rather than the entry rate. The App Store lists it as “SB: Helpdesk, Live Chat & FAQs” from Shark Byte, Inc — the product calls itself HelpCenter, so you will see both names. Rating 4.5 from 243 reviews. Always verify the live price.

answers.q: What is the catch with HelpCenter?
answers.a: The free tier is the hook and the FAQ builder is the reason people stay. But the meter is tickets, not agents: Basic hands you unlimited support staff and then charges $0.16 for every ticket past fifty. At 300 tickets a month that is $45.99, against $19.99 for the Standard tier that includes them outright — so check your own ticket volume before you treat $5.99 as the price. One dependency worth knowing: translating FAQs into other languages is handed off to a separate app (LangShop), so a multilingual store is two subscriptions, not one.

HiBob is genuinely best for growing mid-size companies (roughly 50-500 staff) that have outgrown spreadsheets and want a modern, culture-focused HRIS. Skip it if you're under about 25 employees — a lighter, transparently priced HR tool covers you without the implementation project.

Quote-only, and re-verified as such on 2026-08-17: HiBob publishes no price list, their machine-readable site index lists no pricing page, and neither our July nor our August 2026 capture retrieved an amount. Pricing is per employee per month with modules bolted on, and third-party estimates cluster in the mid-teens per employee per month, plus a one-off implementation fee of roughly 10-20% of the annual contract. Those are estimates, not HiBob's numbers, and the whole thing is negotiated. Get it in writing, including what happens to the per-employee rate as headcount changes mid-term. Always verify the live price.

answers.q: What is the catch with HiBob?
answers.a: Opaque pricing and an implementation fee mean the real cost only surfaces in a sales call — and it's built for scaling mid-size companies, so it's heavy and expensive for a small team.

Hive is genuinely best for project teams that want flexible PM (Gantt, Kanban, forms, chat) and only pay for the modules they actually use. Skip it if you need most of the add-ons anyway (all-inclusive tools price better), or your org demands one standardized suite.

(re-verified 2026-09-03) Free forever for up to 10 workspace members, with 1,000 AI credits a month and 200MB of storage; Starter $5 per user a month and Teams $12 per user a month on yearly billing, which the page states saves 33% against monthly; Enterprise is custom. Read the Starter row before you pay for it: it lifts storage to unlimited and AI credits to 3,000 a month, but it keeps the same 10-member cap as Free and adds a 10-project cap. Only Teams, at $12 with 5,000 AI credits, gives unlimited workspace members. The add-ons are the part to budget: proofing and approvals, timesheets, team resourcing, advanced dashboards, SSO and enterprise controls, and external users each cost $5 per user a month on top, which their own calculator confirms. Two further add-ons, CRM and Finance, are listed on the page with no price at all. The external-user add-on includes 5 external licences per seat. Always verify the live price.

answers.q: What is the catch with Hive?
answers.a: The seat price is honest bait, the add-on grid is the business model: switch on three add-ons and your $12 seat becomes $27 — a la carte flexibility that punishes teams who need the full toolkit. List your must-have modules first and compare the DRESSED price against all-inclusive rivals; for teams needing only core PM, though, Hive is genuinely cheap and pleasant.

Hopp is genuinely best for teams that already travel by ride-hailing and want the spend on one invoice with per-person limits instead of expense claims. Skip it if your team travels where Bolt has thin driver coverage, or you need a published per-ride rate card to budget against.

(price re-verified 2026-09-02 on gethopp.com/en/business/) Hopp Business publishes no subscription price because it does not charge one: the page states there are no activation costs and no minimum commitment, and billing is per ride on a single consolidated monthly invoice. Ride fares vary by city, vehicle class and demand and are not published as a rate card. The site cites 50,000+ businesses; the equivalent Bolt for Business page cites over 70,000 companies. Always verify the live price.

answers.q: What is the catch with Hopp?
answers.a: The honest note is that the platform is free and the rides are not. Hopp Business charges no activation fee and no minimum commitment, so the whole cost is ride pricing, which moves with city, vehicle class and demand — and coverage thins out wherever Bolt does not already run. Check both on your own routes before you move a travel budget across.

Hostinger is genuinely best for budget-conscious owners and side projects that want cheap, decent hosting and will prepay a multi-year term. Skip it if you run a business-critical, high-traffic site — the renewal jump and shared-tier limits make managed hosting the better long-run value.

(re-verified 2026-08-18, read on their own web-hosting and VPS pages) Shared and WordPress hosting runs four tiers on a 48-month term. Premium is $2.99/mo ($143.52 up front, 3 sites, 20 GB SSD) renewing at $10.99. Business is $3.99 ($191.52, 50 sites, 50 GB SSD) renewing at $16.99. Unlimited is $4.99 ($239.52, unlimited sites, 50 GB NVMe) renewing at $17.99. Cloud Startup is $7.99 ($383.52, 100 GB NVMe) renewing at $25.99. VPS is a separate ladder on a 24-month term — KVM 1 at $6.49/mo (1 vCPU, 4 GB RAM, 50 GB NVMe, 4 TB bandwidth) renewing at $11.99, then KVM 2 $8.99 renewing $14.99, KVM 4 $12.99 renewing $28.99 and KVM 8 $25.99 renewing $49.99. Every plan is paid upfront for the whole term, the monthly figure being the total divided by the months, and every plan carries a 30-day money-back guarantee. Both the shared plans and the VPS plans include a free domain for one year. Always verify the live price.

answers.q: What is the catch with Hostinger?
answers.a: The headline price only holds if you prepay years up front — renewals run several times the intro rate, the number-one complaint. Budget for the renewal, and be realistic that budget shared hosting isn't managed-grade performance.

Housecall Pro is genuinely best for home-service businesses (HVAC, plumbing, cleaning) that want scheduling, dispatch, invoicing and payments in one app. Skip it if you're a solo operator who just needs simple invoicing — the field-service features are more than you'll use.

answers.q: How much does Housecall Pro cost?
answers.a: (re-verified 2026-09-04) Basic $59/month billed annually ($79 month-to-month, advertised as 'save $20/mo') for ONE user, with no GPS tracking and no QuickBooks Online sync; Essentials $149/month ($189) for five users; MAX $299/month ($329) for eight users, sold through a demo booking. Extra users beyond those counts are $100/month each on Essentials and $75/month each on MAX — a seat, not a small add-on. There is a 14-day free trial and no credit card is required. Card processing is quoted as 'as low as' 2.59% and bank payments carry a separate 1% fee, so the sticker is the smaller half of the bill: on $40,000 a month of card revenue the processing alone is at least $1,036. Always verify the live price.

answers.q: What is the catch with Housecall Pro?
answers.a: The Basic tier is a trap for real field teams — it omits GPS tracking and QuickBooks sync, so most businesses need Essentials or up. And the seats are the expensive part: users beyond the five on Essentials cost $100 a month each ($75 on MAX), on top of card processing quoted as 'as low as' 2.59% and a 1% fee on bank payments. Price the tier and the headcount you'll actually need.

HubSpot is genuinely best for teams that want marketing, sales, service and content on one contact database and will actually use more than one hub — that shared database is the real product, and it is what makes the price defensible when you use the breadth. Skip it if you need one job done well and cheaply, because a dedicated tool will almost always beat the equivalent HubSpot hub on price; or your contact list is growing fast and your budget is not, since contacts are the meter that moves without you touching anything.

(2026-08-18, read in a live browser on their own marketing pricing page, USD view) Free is $0 for up to 2 users and 1,000 marketing contacts, with no time limit. Starter is advertised at $7 per seat a month against a list price of $20 per seat a month, under a banner reading “Save up to 65% on Starter — new customers only, select offers available for a limited time”. It includes 500 HubSpot Credits and 1,000 marketing contacts. Professional starts at $800 a month paid annually, or $890 a month billed monthly, and includes 3 Core Seats with additional Core Seats from $45 a month, 3,000 credits and 2,000 marketing contacts. On top of that comes a required one-time Professional Onboarding fee of $3,000 that the headline price does not include. Enterprise starts at $3,600 a month with 5 Core Seats, extra seats from $75, 5,000 credits and 10,000 marketing contacts, and a required one-time onboarding fee of $7,000. HubSpot AEO, their answer-engine visibility tracker, is sold separately at $50 a month or $45 annually for 25 prompts across 3 engines, with a 28-day trial. Always verify the live price.

answers.q: What is the catch with HubSpot?
answers.a:
Three numbers on this pricing page are not what they look like, and they compound.

The first is the $7. It is the number in large black type on the Starter card, and the $20 beside it in small grey type is the list price. The banner above the table explains why: up to 65% off Starter, new customers only, for a limited time. So $7 is an introductory rate and $20 is what the seat costs afterwards — a 186% step for a system that by then holds your contact database, which is the single most painful kind of software to leave.

The second is the $800. Professional carries a required one-time onboarding fee of $3,000, disclosed in a footnote under the card rather than in the price. Year one on Professional is therefore $800 × 12 + $3,000 = $12,600 if you pay annually, or $890 × 12 + $3,000 = $13,680 month to month. The onboarding adds roughly a third to the first year, and no amount of shopping around removes it — it is mandatory. Enterprise does the same thing at $7,000 on top of $43,200 a year.

The third is the seat count, because it is not the meter that usually bites. Professional includes 3 Core Seats and 2,000 marketing contacts. For a marketing platform, contacts are the axis that grows on its own: your list gets bigger whether or not you hire anyone, and the contact tier moves the bill without anyone deciding to upgrade. Price your next two years on the list you expect to have, not the team you have now.

One more thing worth knowing before you start on Free. The free tier is genuinely usable — two users, 1,000 contacts, no expiry — and that is exactly how the ladder is designed to work. The step from Starter to Professional is not incremental: at list prices a three-seat team goes from $60 a month to $890 plus $3,000 once, which is roughly fifteen times the monthly cost. Whatever you build on Free, build it knowing where the next rung is.

Hubstaff is genuinely best for agencies and distributed teams that bill clients for hours and need defensible time records — the proof is the product, and per-seat is fair when every seat is a person you invoice for. Skip it if you want to know whether your team is working — that is a management problem and surveillance software makes it worse; also skip it if seats churn a lot, since you pay for every seat you forget to remove.

(2026-08-29, read on their own pricing page) Priced per seat, with both billing columns published. Billed annually: Starter $4.99, Grow $7.50, Team $10, Enterprise $25 per seat per month. Billed monthly: Starter $7, Grow $9, Team $12; Enterprise is sold annually only. The annual column is labelled 'Annual (2 months free)'. Starter, Grow and Team each carry a 2 seat minimum, so the smallest bill Hubstaff will issue is $9.98 a month rather than $4.99. Their FAQ is explicit about what a seat means: 'Hubstaff charges per seat. This means that even if only two out of your three team members are using its tracking features, you will still have to pay for all three members.' Seats added mid-term on an annual plan are prorated — their example is $60 for a seat added in July on a January-to-December plan. Six add-ons are sold per seat per month: Insights, More screenshots, Tasks and Silent app from $2.50, Locations from $3.33, Data retention from $1.67. VIP Support is $29 a month per organisation for accounts spending $275-$400 a month and $59 above $400. There is a 14-day free trial with no credit card, a 30-day money-back guarantee excluding that trial, and a free Project Viewer role for people who only read reports. Re-verified 2026-09-19, reading the plan cards as they render rather than as they ship: every figure above is unchanged — $4.99/$7.50/$10/$25 annual against $7/$9/$12 monthly, the two-seat minimum on the first three tiers, Enterprise annual-only, the six add-on rates, and VIP Support at $29 and $59 per organisation. Two details are worth having: Tasks is included from Grow upward and Locations is not available at all on Starter or Grow, so the add-on menu differs per tier rather than simply costing the same everywhere. The page's plan data still carries a dormant Free tier that does not render as a card and that the FAQ does not acknowledge — asked whether you can use Hubstaff for free, it answers with the 14-day trial. Always verify the live price.

answers.q: What is the catch with Hubstaff?
answers.a: The seat definition is the whole story and they state it plainly, which deserves credit: you pay for every seat you have created, not every person actually being tracked. So an account that grew with your headcount and never got tidied up is billing you for people who left. Audit your seat list before renewal, not after. The second thing is that features on the lower tiers are add-ons rather than inclusions — Insights, Tasks, Silent app and extra screenshots at $2.50 a seat a month, Locations at $3.33 — so the plan you priced and the plan that does what you watched in the demo may differ by ten dollars a seat. And be clear with yourself about why you are buying it: screenshots and activity levels change how a team feels about their work, and that cost does not appear on any pricing page.

IDrive is genuinely best for individuals and small businesses that want cheap multi-device cloud backup with versioning, snapshots and physical seed/restore shipping. Skip it if you need real-time sync-and-collaborate storage (that's Drive/Dropbox territory, not backup), or you won't tolerate the year-two renewal jump.

(2026, re-verified 4 Sep 2026) Free 10 GB Basic tier. IDrive Mini is $0.25/month for 100 GB ($0.83/month for 500 GB). IDrive Personal is $9.99/month for 5 TB, shown discounted to $6.99/month with annual billing (save 30%), scaling up to $99.99/month ($69.99 discounted) at 100 TB. Those are the yearly-billing figures the page opens on; switch it to the Monthly tab and the same Personal 5 TB plan is $11.99/month, and a two-year plan is advertised at up to 50% off the first year. Team starts at the same $9.99/month ($6.99 discounted) for 5 computers and 5 users on 5 TB; Business starts at $19.99/month ($13.99 discounted) for 500 GB with unlimited users. Add-ons: server backup $5/month/server, and Microsoft 365 or Google Workspace backup at $20/seat/year. The honest catch is on the pricing page in IDrive's own words: the discounted price applies to the first year of the selected plan, and standard pricing applies from the second year onward. Two further conditions sit in the same footnotes: going over your storage limit costs $0.25/GB/month on Personal and $0.50/GB/month on Team and Business, and the discount is for new signups only and is not available if you sign up from IDrive's mobile apps. Every figure above read the same on 4 September 2026 as on 27 August 2026. Always verify the live price.

answers.q: What is the catch with IDrive?
answers.a: The first-year price is a teaser and the renewal is the price — IDrive says so itself under the plan table, and on the current numbers the step from discounted to standard is about 43% (Personal 5 TB goes from $6.99 to $9.99 a month). Budget on year-two rates, not the banner, and note that the discount is for new signups only and not available through their mobile apps. Overrun your storage and there is a further $0.25/GB/month on Personal, $0.50 on Team and Business. Beyond that, the honest backup fundamentals apply: a backup you never test-restore is a hope, not a backup, and the first full backup of multi-TB data takes weeks over the wire unless you use their physical Express seed shipping.

Iconosquare is genuinely best for agencies and brands that want deep social analytics, reporting and competitor benchmarking alongside scheduling, especially Instagram-first teams. Skip it if you need a heavy-duty publishing workhorse across many niche platforms, or a single free native analytics view already answers your questions.

(price re-verified 2026-09-15) Read on iconosquare.com/pricing from a Netherlands connection, at the profile count each plan includes. Free covers 2 social profiles, 1 user and 10 posts a month per profile, with one month of analytics history. Starter is €9 a month billed yearly, or €11 month to month, for 3 profiles, 1 user and 30 posts a month. Launch is €33 billed yearly (€39 monthly) for 5 profiles, 1 user and 100 posts. Scale is €69 billed yearly (€83 monthly) and is the first tier with 3 users, unlimited posts, one group and two years of history. Custom starts at €116 billed yearly and covers 5 to unlimited profiles and 1 to unlimited users, with white-label reporting, API access and a dedicated CSM. The page states the yearly saving as €24, €72, €168 and €276 a year. The ladder has changed since our 26 August reading over a US connection, which listed Launch $39, Scale $79 and an Excel tier at $139: Excel no longer appears as a named plan, its price and its white-label, API and CSM features now sit under Custom, and Starter is new below Launch. The profile count is the dial that moves the price, so a quote taken at five says little about what a team managing thirty will pay — and the tiers differ in users, posts and history, not just in profile allowance. Always verify the live price.

answers.q: What is the catch with Iconosquare?
answers.a: Its depth is strongest on Instagram and the core networks; if your priority platform sits outside its best-supported set, coverage thins. Analytics is where it shines — scheduling and community features exist but aren't always as deep as dedicated publishers. And the per-seat, per-profile tiering means agencies managing many brands climb toward the Custom plan quicker than the headline Starter price suggests: Starter and Launch carry one seat, Scale three, and only Custom lifts the five-profile ceiling.

InVideo is genuinely best for marketing teams and creators who want to turn a prompt or script into a publish-ready first-draft video fast, using templates, AI voiceover and stock. Skip it if you need frame-level creative control, long-form or highly bespoke production, or your usage would blow past the monthly credit allowance.

Four paid tiers plus a free plan, read on invideo.io/pricing on 5 September 2026. On annual billing: Plus $17 a month (750 AI credits a year), Max $85 a month (3,900 credits), Generative $170 a month (8,000 credits) and Elite $900 a month (42,500 credits); month-to-month the same tiers are $20, $100, $200 and $1,000. Credits are the meter: every AI generation, avatar minute and export draws them down, and the annual pool is what you actually buy. Always verify the live price.

answers.q: What is the catch with InVideo?
answers.a: The honest catch is the credit model — each plan is a fixed monthly credit allowance that different models consume at different rates, and unused credits do not roll over, so a heavy month can exhaust an allowance long before it renews while a slow month simply wastes what you paid for. There is also no free way in any more: on 31 August 2026 the pricing page published no free tier at all, so the cheapest route to trying it is the Plus plan at $20 a month. AI video is fast but generic by default: templated output needs real editing and brand direction to not look like everyone else's. Treat it as a first-draft engine, not a finished-studio replacement.

InboxAlly is genuinely best for serious senders — email marketers and cold-outreach teams — whose deliverability problems are costing measurable revenue and who need active reputation repair. Skip it if you're a small sender who just needs basic list hygiene (cheaper warm-up tools suffice), or your inbox issues stem from content and list quality you haven't fixed.

(price re-verified 2026-08-31 against the vendor's own pricing page, read from a European exit) Every amount unchanged and confirmed on the plan comparison table, which states 'Pricing in USD, billed monthly': Starter $149/mo (100 seed emails/day, 1 sender profile), Plus $645/mo (500/day, 5 profiles), Premium $1,190/mo (1,000/day, 10 profiles), Enterprise custom (custom volume, unlimited profiles, dedicated deliverability experts). 10-day free trial, no card. No annual billing option is offered. Premium's sessions, more precisely than the previous dossier: a 1-hour setup/strategy session plus weekly 30-minute progress reviews. VENDOR SELF-CONTRADICTION, confirm before relying: the tier cards give Starter 'Email support' and reserve live chat for Plus and above, while the comparison table lower on the same page ticks 'Live chat support' and 'Dedicated CSM' for all four tiers including Starter. Phone & Zoom support, the setup session and the weekly reviews are consistently Premium-and-above in both places. Every plan includes IA Score, IA Reputation, Adaptive Autowarmup, the in-app IA Assistant, the full REST API, native CRM integrations and inbox placement testing. Always verify the live price.

answers.q: What is the catch with InboxAlly?
answers.a: This is a premium, seed-list-based deliverability tool, and the price reflects it — Starter alone is well above casual warm-up apps, so it only makes sense if inbox placement is genuinely costing you real revenue. It improves sender reputation through engagement signals, but it's not a magic fix for bad content or a purchased list: deliverability still depends on how you actually send. Buy it when the math (lost revenue from spam-foldering) clearly beats the monthly fee.

Increff is genuinely best for retail brands and omnichannel sellers at real scale needing warehouse management plus algorithm-driven merchandising and inventory optimization. Skip it if you're a small or single-channel store where simpler inventory software suffices, or you can't commit to an enterprise implementation.

No public pricing, re-verified 2026-09-14 and consistent across every reading we have. Increff's own /pricing URL still returns a 404, and our monthly captures of the site from July to September 2026 produced no amount at all. Increff prices every deal case by case, scaled to the operation — warehouses, users and which modules you take (WMS, merchandising) — which their partnership team confirmed to us directly on 28 Jul 2026. There are no published tiers to compare, so budget for an enterprise implementation and ask for a tailored quote. Always verify the live price.

answers.q: What is the catch with Increff?
answers.a: This is enterprise omnichannel supply-chain software, and the opaque, quote-based pricing signals the target customer: retail brands with real scale, not small stores. The value — algorithmic merchandising and inventory optimization — only pays off at a catalog and volume large enough for those optimizations to move money. For a small or mid seller, it's likely more platform (and cost and implementation) than the problem warrants. For a scaling omnichannel brand, it's built for exactly that.

Influencer Hero is genuinely best for brands running influencer marketing as a continuous programme rather than a campaign, with enough volume to use 1,000 reach-outs a month from the first month, who want discovery, outreach, a creator CRM, UGC tracking and affiliate management in one place instead of a spreadsheet plus four tools. Skip it if you want to test the channel before committing, because the three-month minimum makes the real entry price $1,557 rather than $519; you are a two-person team on Standard's single seat; or you pay creators at any scale, since 20 payouts a month is the cap until you reach $839.

answers.q: How much does Influencer Hero cost?
answers.a:
(pricing matrix read 18 September 2026 in documentation the vendor sent us; the public ladder at influencer-hero.com/pricing was read the same week and shows the quarterly column) Four plans, and the figure you see depends entirely on the billing term you pick. Billed monthly: Standard $649, Pro $1,049, Business $2,490. Billed quarterly: $519, $839 and $1,992 — and this is the column the public pricing page leads with, which is why $519 is the number most people quote. Billed annually: $454, $734 and $1,743. The advertised 20% and 30% savings check out exactly against the monthly rate ($649 × 0.8 = $519.20, × 0.7 = $454.30), so the discounts are real and the headline is simply the discounted one.

What each plan carries: Standard is one seat, 1,000 reach-outs a month and 20 influencer payouts. Pro is three seats, 5,000 reach-outs and 200 payouts. Business is eight seats, 10,000 reach-outs and 500 payouts — the pricing page contradicts itself here. The Business plan card lists unlimited influencer payouts, but the Compare all features grid further down the same page reads 20, 200, 500 and Unlimited across Standard, Pro, Business and Enterprise on the row Number of influencer payouts, which puts Business at 500 and matches the figure in the documentation the vendor sent us. Read in a browser on 19 September 2026. Two of the three readings say 500, so that is the number to plan for, and it is worth having in writing. Enterprise is custom on every axis. Every plan carries a three-month minimum term and there is no free trial, so the smallest real commitment is three months of Standard: $1,947 billed monthly, or $1,557 if you take the quarterly rate. The influencer CRM, the outreach automation and the UGC tracking are in every plan; the ladder is gated on quota and seats. Influencer payouts run through bank debit at 0.1% to 0.4%, against the 2-3% that card processors typically charge. Always verify the live price.

answers.q: What is the catch with Influencer Hero?
answers.a:
The three-month minimum is the real commitment, and there is no free trial to soften it. Every plan carries it, so the smallest honest entry price is not $519 but three months — $1,557 on the quarterly rate, $1,947 if you pay monthly. An influencer programme takes longer than four weeks to show you anything, so the vendor is not being unreasonable; it just means the decision is a quarter of spending rather than a month of trying.

Read which column you are quoted. The public pricing page leads with the quarterly rate, so $519 is what gets repeated — but billed monthly the same plan is $649, a quarter more. Pro is $839 or $1,049, Business $1,992 or $2,490. The 20% and 30% savings are genuine and check out exactly against the monthly rate; the trap is only that the advertised number already has the discount in it.

What the ladder actually meters is worth understanding, because it is better than it looks. A reach-out counts once, at the moment you first contact a new influencer. Every follow-up, reply and ongoing conversation with that same creator after that is unlimited and never draws the quota down again — so the meter counts new relationships opened, not messages sent. Standard's 1,000 a month is therefore 1,000 new creators, which is a great many, and nurturing the ones who answer costs nothing.

Hitting the cap gives you two routes and the vendor recommends one of them against its own short-term interest: buy a top-up, or move up a tier. Their own documentation says brands who top up once tend to keep doing it, so repeated top-ups erode the saving from staying low. No top-up rate is published anywhere, which is the one number still missing from an otherwise unusually open account.

One inconsistency to check before you sign, and it sits on the vendor's own page. The Business plan card lists unlimited influencer payouts; the comparison grid lower down that same page reads 20, 200, 500 and Unlimited across the four plans, putting Business at 500 — which is also what the documentation the vendor sent us says. Read in a browser on 19 September 2026. Two of the three readings give 500, so plan for 500 rather than unlimited, and on a plan at $1,992 a month get it in writing before you sign.

Seats follow the quota — one, three, eight — so a two-person team is pushed to Pro by headcount alone, whatever its volume.

Insightful is genuinely best for COOs, CFOs and operations leaders who want a work intelligence platform rather than a time clock: workforce analytics plus AI process capture — where the hours go, and how the work actually flows — across in-office and remote teams. Skip it if you value a low-surveillance culture, run a tiny team, or need a monthly price you can compare up front — month-to-month billing exists on select plans, but every rate on the pricing page is the annual one.

(price re-verified 2026-09-09 against the vendor's own pricing page) (2026) Per seat; the rates below are the annual ones. Workforce Analytics $8/seat/mo, Workflow Optimization $12/seat/mo (a beta open to selected customers), or both bundled at $16/seat/mo (saves 20%); Enterprise custom, and that is where audit logs and SSO sit. Add-ons: Workspace Security $4/seat/mo, screen recording $4, on-demand screenshots $4, higher-frequency screenshots $3 (up to 120 an hour), data-warehouse integration $0.50 for the whole bundle of custom API access, BigQuery and Snowflake. The page adds one line under the plan cards: month-to-month billing is available on select plans, without naming a monthly rate. A 7-day free trial gives full access except Automatic Time Mapping, no card. Admin, manager and client users are not billed unless you also track them, and users added mid-cycle are prorated. On-premise deployment requires at least 250 licences. Always verify the live price.

answers.q: What is the catch with Insightful?
answers.a: This is employee-monitoring software, so weigh the culture cost, not just the price: the advertised $8-16 rates are per seat AND are the annual ones (month-to-month exists on select plans but is never priced), security features like insider-threat detection are a paid add-on, and monitoring tools can damage trust if rolled out without transparency.

Instapage is genuinely best for marketing teams running significant paid ad campaigns who need post-click optimisation — AdMap ad-to-page personalisation, A/B testing and heatmaps. Skip it if you run limited ad campaigns or want budget pricing — at $99+/mo it's overkill below real paid-traffic volume.

(re-verified 4 Sep 2026) Instapage does publish plan prices; they are not on the URL we had recorded. instapage.com/en/pricing redirects to the homepage at instapage.com/lp, and the plan table sits at instapage.com/plans. Our 26 August reading landed on the redirect, found no figures and concluded that prices had been withdrawn; the figures below match the last published rates this dossier already held, so the more likely explanation is a moved page rather than a withdrawal. Three tiers sit there. Create is $99 a month month-to-month or $79 billed annually, for 15,000 unique monthly visitors. Optimize is $199 or $159 annually for 30,000 unique monthly visitors, with selectors for 50,000 and for a custom volume — the custom option defaults to 50,000 and hands you to sales. Convert is quote-only. Annual billing is advertised as 'save up to 20%', and every tier carries unlimited contacts. The 14-day free trial asks for a credit card and is capped at 2,500 unique monthly visitors; Instapage's own FAQ states that exceeding that cap ends the trial automatically and moves you onto the paid plan you selected. Always verify the live price.

answers.q: What is the catch with Instapage?
answers.a: It's premium-priced and only justified by serious ad spend — Create is $79 a month billed annually for 15,000 unique monthly visitors, and the price per thousand barely improves as you climb, so the higher tiers buy features rather than cheaper traffic. The 14-day trial needs a card and carries its own cap of 2,500 visitors; crossing it ends the trial and starts the paid plan by itself. And there's the ownership question the feature list does not raise: publishing to your own domain means pointing a CNAME at Instapage — their help centre carries a per-registrar guide for exactly that — so the page is served by them and lives as long as the subscription does. Their own docs add a second catch worth knowing before you standardise on it: “we lock domains under the first Instapage account that uses them”. Treat these pages as rented campaign infrastructure, not as part of your site, and keep the copy somewhere you control.

Intelis is genuinely best for Shopify stores with hundreds to a few thousand variants that genuinely compete on price on Google Shopping and want competitor monitoring and repricing handled automatically. Skip it if your catalogue is small, you do not compete primarily on price, or your variant count sits just above a tier boundary and would push you to the next rung for a handful of SKUs.

(re-verified 8 September 2026 on apps.shopify.com/ecoprice-analytics, intelis.ai/pricing and the Intelis homepage) Four tiers on the Shopify listing, priced by how many products or variants you track, each with a 14-day free trial. Basic $49 a month or $490 a year, a 17% saving: up to 100 products or variants, Google Shopping competitor monitoring, AI automatch for unlimited competitors, dynamic pricing, unlimited competitor URL tracking, reports, pricing history and chat support. Professional $179 a month or $1,790 a year: up to 1,000, adding variant tracking, sales analysis, live feed export, pricing strategy monitoring, an AI assistant and premium chat support. Premium $249 a month or $2,490 a year: up to 2,000, adding Shopify Markets support per market, Google Analytics integration and API access. Business $399 a month or $3,990 a year: up to 5,000, adding a custom labels feed for Google Merchant Center, MAP monitoring, a customised AI matching algorithm, pricing consultation, advanced analytics and A+ support. The vendor's own pages used to disagree with the listing above Premium -- on 21 August 2026 intelis.ai/pricing showed Business at $499 with a $4,990 annual rate and Enterprise at $849, while the homepage said $749. That is now resolved: on 8 September 2026 the pricing page and the homepage both show Business at $399 ($3,990 a year) and Enterprise at $749 ($7,490 a year) for up to 10,000 SKUs, matching the listing. The vendor's own pages count SKUs where the listing counts products or variants. All charges are billed in USD and recur every 30 days. Developer Intelis; the app launched 6 July 2021 and carries a 4.9 rating from 101 reviews. Always verify the live price.

answers.q: What is the catch with Intelis?
answers.a:
The ladder counts variants, not products, and that is where stores get caught. A catalogue of forty garments in five sizes and three colours is six hundred variants, so a shop most people would call small lands on the $179 tier rather than the $49 one. Count your variants, not your line items, before you read the price.

The vendor's own numbers above Premium used to contradict each other, and that is worth knowing mainly because it has been fixed. On 21 August 2026 the Shopify listing said Business was $399 while intelis.ai/pricing said $499 with a $4,990 annual rate, and the homepage and the pricing page gave Enterprise as $749 and $849. Re-read on 8 September 2026, all three pages agree: Business $399 ($3,990 a year), Enterprise $749 ($7,490) for up to 10,000 SKUs. If you are working from a comparison written earlier this year, check its figures against the listing.

And automatic repricing is not a switch you leave alone. The matching is AI-driven across Google Shopping and competitor sites, and a mismatched listing quietly reprices the wrong product, while an unbounded rule set on a busy category is how a store races itself to the bottom. Set floor prices before you turn dynamic pricing on, and audit what the automatch decided in the first fortnight.

Jibble is genuinely best for teams that need attendance records without a per-seat bill — if the free tier covers your case it is genuinely free, which nothing else in this category offers. Skip it if you need the paid features, because you will have to get those prices from them directly; also skip facial recognition without checking your local rules on biometric data, which is a legal question rather than a pricing one.

(read 2026-08-30 on jibble.io, re-checked 2026-09-19) There is no published price for anything above the free plan. The pricing page has been retired: jibble.io/pricing returns a 301 to /upgrade-plans, which returns a 301 to the homepage, and /plans does the same. What the homepage claims is a free forever plan with unlimited users, described as '100% free', with no credit card required and setup 'in under 2 minutes'. Where a price table would be, an impact calculator projects annual savings on three published assumptions — 40 hours a week, 48 working weeks a year, 5.5% payroll leakage — and labels the cost of Jibble Free as $0. The enterprise page names no figure either; its only call to action is a demo booking. (2026-09-02) Jibble's partnerships team confirmed to us in writing, through the PartnerStack programme, that there is no external pricing page. Jibble states an average of 4.8 out of 5 across major review platforms and app stores on more than 20,000 verified reviews. Re-checked 19 September 2026: jibble.io/pricing, /plans and /upgrade-plans all still land on the homepage, no paid tier is named anywhere on the public site, and the FAQ now spells out what free covers — desktop time tracking, mobile and web clock-ins, basic timesheets and integrations with Slack, Microsoft Teams and QuickBooks, “at no cost, forever”. Always verify the live price.

answers.q: What is the catch with Jibble?
answers.a: Free forever with unlimited users is a real claim and unusual in this category, where per-seat pricing is the norm — that alone makes it worth a look for a team on a tight budget. Two things to establish before you rely on it. First, what the free tier actually excludes, because 'unlimited users' and 'unlimited features' are different promises and the paid tiers exist for a reason. Second, note that their pricing page leads with a calculator showing what you supposedly save rather than what you pay. That is a marketing choice, and the number it produces rests on assumptions about payroll leakage that are theirs, not measured in your business.

Joiin is genuinely best for finance teams and accountants consolidating multi-entity, multi-currency group reporting from Xero, QuickBooks or Sage without hand-built spreadsheets. Skip it if you run a single entity (your accounting platform's own reports cover it), or your ledgers live outside the supported integrations and you'd be importing spreadsheets anyway.

(re-verified 2026-08-17 against Joiin's own machine-readable pricing page) 14-day free trial, no credit card; unlimited users and reports on every plan. Priced by the number of companies you consolidate, with the page showing both columns: monthly against annual, per month. 1 company $28 / $23, 2 $36 / $29, 5 $70 / $57, 10 $111 / $92, 20 $167 / $139, 50 $217 / $174, 100 $336 / $252. Above 100 companies it starts from $336/mo plus $2.80 per additional company. Paying monthly runs roughly 20% above the annual rate at every step. Always verify the live price.

answers.q: What is the catch with Joiin?
answers.a: The $23 headline covers a single company on annual billing — but consolidation is the whole point of Joiin, and a real group of 10-20 entities lands at $92-139 a month. Month-to-month billing adds roughly two months per year. And it consolidates only what its integrations reach — nine ledgers, from Xero, QuickBooks and Sage to Pennylane, Puzzle, FreeAgent, Zoho Books, Fortnox and MYOB — so anything outside that list arrives as a spreadsheet import you repeat every month.

answers.q: Is Jotform AI Agents worth it?
answers.a: Jotform AI Agents is genuinely best for teams already using Jotform (or wanting no-code) that need AI chatbots and service agents to handle leads, support and bookings tied to their forms. Skip it if you need a deeply customizable, standalone conversational-AI platform, or your conversation volume would make the per-tier caps expensive.

answers.q: How much does Jotform AI Agents cost?
answers.a: (re-verified 4 Sep 2026 on jotform.com/ai/agents/pricing, on the yearly tab; the same figures were read from a US exit on 26 Aug 2026. The page localises its currency — it quotes $34 / $39 / $99 to a US visitor and €34 / €39 / €99 to a Dutch one, the same numerals either way.) Starter is free. Bronze is $34 a month, Silver $39 and Gold $99, each billed annually, with 'save up to 20%' against monthly billing; Enterprise is quoted. On the AI Agents page the ladder is drawn in agents and conversations, not in forms and submissions: 5 agents and 100 monthly conversations on Starter, 25 and 1,000 on Bronze, 50 and 2,500 on Silver, 100 and 10,000 on Gold. Sessions, voice-call minutes, SMS and knowledge-base characters are metered alongside — 10,000 / 100,000 / 1,000,000 / 2,000,000 monthly sessions and 50 / 100 / 200 / 300 voice minutes across the same four tiers. Jotform defines a session as a chatbot view, a page refresh or a phone call starting, whether or not anyone interacts. Always verify the live price.

answers.q: What is the catch with Jotform AI Agents?
answers.a: The gating detail is conversations, not features — Starter's 100 a month is a few days on a live site, and an agent that actually gets used will push you up a tier. Sessions are metered separately and Jotform counts a chatbot view or a page refresh as one, so a busy page burns allowance without ever holding a conversation; voice minutes and SMS meter on top as well. It's also tightly bound to the Jotform ecosystem: brilliant if you already live in Jotform forms, less compelling as a standalone chatbot if you don't. For form-driven support and lead capture, it's a fast, low-code win.

Jubilee is genuinely best for bankruptcy attorneys and legal professionals who want streamlined petition preparation, document automation and case management for filings. Skip it if you don't practice bankruptcy law, or you file so few cases that a general practice-management tool plus manual forms is enough.

Pay As You Go is $95 per case. The alternative is an annual subscription billed by yearly filing volume. Jubilee 36 is $995/yr (up to 36 filings, 2 users, $34.99/case over) and Jubilee 150 $2,495/yr (up to 150, 3 users, $26.99 over). Jubilee 300 is $3,995/yr (up to 300, 3 users, $17.99 over) and Jubilee 500 $4,995/yr (up to 500, 5 users, $12.99 over). Prices are for annual billing; above 500 filings a year the vendor quotes custom pricing (re-verified 2026-08-26). Always verify the live price.

answers.q: What is the catch with Jubilee?
answers.a: It's a focused vertical tool — bankruptcy petition preparation and case management — so its whole value is bounded by that practice area; a general legal practice won't get much from it. The case-count tiers are the thing to size correctly: pick 36 vs 300 by your real annual filing volume, and check whether the pay-per-case option is cheaper if you file sporadically. For a bankruptcy practice, the automation and court-form handling are exactly the point.

Kartra is genuinely best for creators and coaches who want funnels, email, checkout, memberships and scheduling under one roof instead of five subscriptions. Skip it if you only need one of those pieces — a dedicated tool does that piece better and cheaper than an all-in-one.

(re-verified 2026-09-05 on their own pricing page) Four tiers, monthly against yearly: Essentials $59 / $52, Starter $119 / $99, Growth $229 / $189 and Professional $549 / $429, with yearly billing advertised as saving up to 22% and a 14-day trial. The tier names moved since our August reading — the $119 plan is now called Starter and the $229 plan Growth — while every amount stayed the same. The line that changes the arithmetic and is missing from most summaries: Essentials charges a 5% transaction fee on your sales, and the tiers above it charge 0%. On $10,000 a month of sales that fee is $500, which makes the $60 step from Essentials to Starter trivially worth taking. Contacts are capped at 500, 2,500, 12,500 and 25,000 across the four tiers; Essentials sends 10,000 emails and texts a month against unlimited above it and includes 1 custom domain. Kartra never blocks new leads: it upgrades you automatically to the tier that fits and charges a mid-cycle reconciliation fee for the move — two answers above that one, the same FAQ says a Kartra subscription is flat-rate and there are never any extra fees. Always verify the live price.

answers.q: What is the catch with Kartra?
answers.a: If your core need is polished course delivery, Kajabi's creator features are stronger; Kartra wins on all-in-one breadth, not course depth.

Katana MRP is genuinely best for product makers and small manufacturers who need live inventory, production scheduling and multi-channel order sync in one cloud platform. Skip it if you're a simple reseller who doesn't manufacture (a plain inventory tool is cheaper), or your volume is too low to justify the add-on-driven real cost.

answers.q: How much does Katana MRP cost?
answers.a: (re-verified 2026-09-14) A Free plan covering 30 SKUs with unlimited users, integrations and locations plus all features, add-ons and API access, then Core starting at $299/mo with unlimited SKUs and users and 24/7 support, and an Advantage tier on custom pricing. The $299 is a floor, not a bill: Katana's own price calculator, embedded on the pricing page, charges per delivered sales order on a tapering rate — $0.1440 per order at 500 a month ($72), $0.1040 at 2,000 ($208) and $0.0594 at 8,000 ($475) — and Core includes one inventory location, with extras at $49 each for a single extra, $42 each at two and $31 each at five. The add-ons are priced separately: manufacturing routings and insights $199/mo, end-to-end traceability via batch or serial numbers $249/mo, and warehouse management with bin locations and pick-and-pack $149/mo. Onboarding is a $2,000 option on Core and included on Advantage. Annual billing costs MORE per month rather than less: it adds a "scale guarantee" line — $23, $54 and $79 a month on the vendor's own three example configurations — that covers 20% more orders and locations than your estimate. Those three worked examples land at $654, $823 and $1,110 a month billed monthly, and $677, $902 and $1,164 billed annually. Always verify the live price.

answers.q: What is the catch with Katana MRP?
answers.a: The $299 headline is the floor. Production routings and traceability are paid add-ons on top, and those are exactly the features most manufacturers need, which is why real bills often land two to three times higher. Cost also rises with sales-order volume, so a busy month is a bigger month. It's genuinely capable manufacturing software; just price the add-ons you need, not the base plan.

Keap is genuinely best for service-based small businesses, coaches and solopreneurs who want CRM, email, payments and automation in one tool — and will invest the time to learn it. Skip it if you're price-sensitive, want a modern UI, or only need simple email — the cost and learning curve bite.

Starting at $299/mo billed monthly for the whole platform, with no feature-based tiers and no free plan (re-verified 2026-09-05 on their own pricing page). That $299 is what the calculator quotes for its own minimum: 2 users and 1,500 contacts. Raising only the contact count on the same calculator gives $335 at 2,500, $449 at 5,000, $539 at 10,000 and $719 at 25,000, and users beyond the first two are $39 a month each. Keap also requires paid implementation services — strategy consulting, data import and migration — quoted separately before you go live. Text marketing is bundled at Tier 1 (500 messages and 100 voice minutes) and steps to $24, $39, $79, $139 and $279 a month above that, with overages at $0.015 a message and $0.01 a voice minute; it is US-only. Cancelling an annual contract before its term ends carries a $299 early termination fee, and cancellation must be started by phone at least ten days before the next invoice date. Keap has been acquired by Thryv; its own pages now route training to Thryv Academy. Always verify the live price.

answers.q: What is the catch with Keap?
answers.a: Cost is the big one (56% of reviewers flag it), the interface feels dated, and there's a real 2–4 week learning curve on the automation builder. Billing and cancellation complaints are common — their own terms carry a $299 early termination fee on an annual contract and require ten days' phone notice — and email design is thinner than dedicated email tools.

Keeper Security is genuinely best for teams that need shared credentials with real admin control and audit, and that will genuinely use the provisioning and role-based access that separate this from a consumer password manager. Skip it if you are under five people wanting a shared vault, since Business Starter is scoped at 5-10 users and Keeper's own Personal plan at $42.99 a year, or Family at $91.99, covers that case for less.

answers.q: How much does Keeper Security cost?
answers.a: (re-verified 2026-09-17 on their own business and add-on pricing pages, reading the US price list) Three business tiers, all billed annually: Business Starter at $2.00 per user per month ($24 a year), described as protection for 5-10 users; Business at $4.00 per user per month ($48 a year); Enterprise at $6.00 per user per month ($72 a year), sold through Request a Quote. The amounts are injected by script, so a page fetched without rendering shows the tiers with the figures missing. Personal and family plans are priced on their own page: Personal (Keeper Unlimited) $42.99 billed annually and Family $91.99 billed annually. CURRENCY WARNING, corrected 2026-09-17: the same pages served to a Dutch visitor carry a different euro list, not a conversion of the dollar one — Business Starter €2.00 and Business €4.00 match, but Enterprise is €5.50 against $6.00, Personal €52.02 against $42.99 and Family €111.31 against $91.99. The dossier previously carried those last two euro figures as dollar amounts. The add-ons carry their own list, also in US dollars: BreachWatch and KeeperChat $24 per user per year (€22 on the euro list), Advanced Reporting & Alerts and Compliance Reports $12 per user per year (€11), Endpoint Privilege Manager $36 per endpoint per year, Secure File Storage from $132 per year for 100GB (€108), Professional Services from $270 per year, with Connection Manager and Keeper Secrets Manager priced only on request. Always verify the live price.

answers.q: What is the catch with Keeper Security?
answers.a: The per-user price is the smallest part of the bill. Read the add-ons page next to the plan page and the shape becomes clear: BreachWatch and KeeperChat are $24 per user per year each, Advanced Reporting & Alerts and Compliance Reports $12 per user per year each, endpoint privilege management $36 per endpoint per year — so a Business seat at $4.00 a month can quietly double once you add the monitoring and reporting most buyers assume is included, and Connection Manager and Secrets Manager are not even priced. Annual billing is stated on every tier, so there is no month-to-month option to test with, and Business Starter is scoped at 5–10 users. Ask for the base plan and each add-on you need as separate lines, because a bundled quote here hides which part is actually costing you.

Kinsta is genuinely best for business-critical WordPress sites where speed, uptime and expert support directly affect revenue. Skip it if you run a small, low-traffic site on a tight budget — entry-level shared hosting or a caching plugin gets you most of the way for a fraction of the price.

(re-verified 2026-09-14 on their own plans page, USD, tax excluded) Managed WordPress hosting from $35/mo for a single site, or $30/mo billed annually at $350 a year, with the first month free on top — Kinsta advertises annual as two months off. That entry plan carries one WordPress install, 10GB storage, 20GB server bandwidth, 125GB CDN bandwidth and 14 days of backup retention, and you choose whether it is metered on bandwidth or on visits, which is a real change from the visit-only plans older reviews describe. The multi-site ladder runs WP 2 at $70/mo or $59 billed annually ($700 a year), WP 5 at $115 or $96 ($1,150), WP 10 at $225 or $188 ($2,250), WP 20 at $340 or $284 ($3,400) and WP 40 at $450 or $375 ($4,500). Agency plans start at that same $340/mo, or $284 billed annually. Above them sits an Enterprise line our earlier readings missed entirely: it starts at $500/mo, or $417 billed annually, with $5,000 payable on signup. Several things that look like plan features are priced separately — dedicated servers from $300/mo, PHP performance at $10 per 500MB a month, external backups to AWS or Google Cloud at $2 per site a month plus $1 per GB, and more frequent backups at $20 a site for six-hourly or $100 for hourly. It is a premium tier — cheaper shared hosts exist. There is no exclusive discount code to look for: Kinsta confirmed to us on 28 Jul 2026 that it gives no partner-only or affiliate-only discounts. Always verify the live price.

answers.q: What is the catch with Kinsta?
answers.a: You're paying a premium for managed speed, Google Cloud infrastructure and expert support — worth it if performance and hands-off management matter, wasteful on a low-traffic hobby site a $5 shared host would carry fine.

Kit is genuinely best for creators, writers and coaches building an audience-first business who want email, landing pages, digital products and a creator network in one. Skip it if you're an e-commerce store (commerce-native email tools fit better) or your list is big-but-cold — clean it before paying per subscriber.

(re-verified 2026-09-02) The free plan is $0/mo and covers up to 10,000 email subscribers, with unlimited landing pages and forms, unlimited email broadcasts, audience tagging and segmentation, and digital products and subscriptions. Kit renamed the old Newsletter plan to Free and took automation out of it: Visual Automations and email sequences are now Creator-and-above, and Kit's affiliate briefing of 2 September 2026 adds that new free accounts open with a 14-day Creator trial and that accounts already on the Newsletter plan keep what they had. Creator is $39/mo billed monthly, or $33/mo billed yearly ($390 a year, saving $78), and adds unlimited Visual Automations, unlimited email sequences, Kit MCP, SMS marketing and branding removal. Pro — the tier that adds Subscriber Signals, engagement analytics, deliverability reporting, a newsletter referral system and unlimited users — is $79/mo billed monthly, or $66/mo billed yearly ($790 a year, saving $158). Paying yearly saves 17%. Every paid price on the page is quoted for 1,000 email subscribers and Kit bills by list size, so read the tier for your own list before you budget. Paid plans open with a 14-day free trial without a card, and migrations are free. Always verify the live price.

answers.q: What is the catch with Kit?
answers.a: Three honest notes. Subscriber-based pricing counts everyone on your list — cold subscribers cost the same as fans, so prune before you price. The free plan changed shape in 2026: it now runs to 10,000 subscribers rather than 1,000 (re-verified 2026-09-02), but Visual Automations and email sequences came out of it, so the free tier sends and captures without automating anything — what puts you on Creator at $39/mo, or $33/mo paid yearly, is wanting a welcome sequence rather than list growth. And the 35% price hike in 2025 changed the value math: the free tier is still arguably the best in creator email, but paid tiers now deserve comparison shopping rather than default loyalty. The creator-first features (tip jars, paid newsletters, recommendations) remain the real differentiator.

Kite is genuinely best for shopify stores that want the discount mechanics themselves — gift with purchase, buy X get Y, tiered and volume pricing, with progress bars pushing the cart toward the next reward — built on native Shopify Functions rather than theme edits. Skip it if your promotions are simple enough for Shopify's own discount engine, or you are on Advanced or Plus and unwilling to start at $49 — and if all you need is a pile of unique codes, a code generator does that for a third of the price.

(prices read 2026-09-06 on apps.shopify.com/kite-free-gift) Four plans, billed in USD every 30 days. The Free plan is free to install and covers the first 50 discount orders each month; the listing states that $29 a month is billed only if you go over 50 orders. Starter is $29 a month, or $299 a year at a stated 14% saving, and adds unlimited discount orders, combined offers, progress bars and up to 10K bulk codes. Growth is $49 a month, or $499 a year at 15%, and raises bulk codes to 100K with multiple rules per offer and campaign links. Pro is $99 a month, or $999 a year at 16%, and adds custom discount functions, checkout gifts (Plus only) and segment targeting. The three paid tiers carry a 7-day free trial. Free and Starter both say 'Not for Shopify Advanced and Plus'. Always verify the live price.

answers.q: What is the catch with Kite?
answers.a: 'Free to install' is doing a lot of work on this listing. The free plan covers the first 50 discount orders a month, and the same panel says $29 a month is billed once you pass them — so it is a threshold with an invoice behind it, not a free tier you can settle on. A store running one decent promotion will cross 50 discounted orders in days and be on Starter money without choosing to upgrade. The second catch is written on the plans themselves: Free and Starter are both labelled 'Not for Shopify Advanced and Plus', so if you are on either of those Shopify plans your real entry price is the $49 Growth tier, not the $29 the listing leads with. And the feature most likely to sell the app to a large merchant — free gifts added at checkout — is marked Plus only and sits in the $99 Pro tier, which means the Plus stores it is built for pay $1,188 a year to reach it.

Kiwi Sizing is genuinely best for apparel and accessory stores where sizing drives returns, and that want charts plus an AI fit recommender without building either — 4.7 stars from 1,216 reviews on 19 September 2026 is a genuinely strong base, though the recent ones read differently from the aggregate. Skip it if you sell one-size or non-wearable products, where a size chart answers a question nobody asks, or you need more than ten charts and would land on a tier whose order-volume charges are not published.

answers.q: How much does Kiwi Sizing cost?
answers.a: (read 5 September 2026 and re-read 19 September 2026 on apps.shopify.com/kiwi-sizing, no amount changed) Four tiers, and the interesting line is not the price but the sentence under it. Free publishes up to three size charts with 22 templates and unlimited CSV import, and puts a Kiwi watermark on your storefront. Premium is $7.99 a month for up to ten charts, removes the watermark, adds Google Analytics and auto-translation into English and Spanish, and states plainly: no additional monthly charges. Plus, the tier the store marks Popular, is $14.99 for up to twenty charts, ten size recommenders and six languages. Ultimate is $26.99 for unlimited charts and recommenders and 22 languages. Both Plus and Ultimate carry the same caveat that Premium does not: additional charges apply based on order volume, and the listing does not say what those charges are. Import credits are an optional add-on on every paid tier, and all three come with a 14-day free trial. The listing adds that all charges are billed in USD and that recurring and usage-based charges are billed every 30 days. So the cheapest paid plan is the only one whose bill you can predict, and the one the store pushes is not. Always verify the live price.

answers.q: What is the catch with Kiwi Sizing?
answers.a: The free plan is not limited by the chart count most people assume. Three charts is generous for a small catalogue; the real limit is the Kiwi watermark sitting on your storefront, and removing it is what the $7.99 buys. Judge the free tier on whether you can live with that watermark in front of customers, not on how many charts you get. And read the small print above Plus and Ultimate before you upgrade: both add order-volume charges that the App Store listing never quantifies, while Premium says in writing that it has none.

Kixie is genuinely best for outbound sales teams living in their CRM that want a serious power dialer with local presence, SMS and automation. Skip it if low call volumes (per-seat + minutes math won't pay back), or you want monthly flexibility without contract fine print.

(2026-09-10, read on their own pricing page) No seat price is published. Three plans are listed — Professional, Single-Line PowerDialer and Multi-Line PowerDialer — and no amount is rendered anywhere on the page; the billing toggle that used to sit above the cards has gone too, so there is now no path from this page to a number. The core phone system is identical on all three; what separates them is dialling. There is no PowerDialer on Professional, one line on Single-Line, and up to four simultaneous lines on Multi-Line — also the only tier offering AI human voice detection, as a premium add-on. ConnectionBoost, Conversation Intelligence and DNC compliance are add-ons at every tier. The plan cards claim unlimited US/Canada minutes while the FAQ published in the page's own structured data prices unlimited US and Canada minutes at $30 a month per user, so which of the two applies belongs in writing in your quote. First US/Canada number free, extra local numbers $5.00 a month, porting in free. Texts from $0.011 each ($11 per 1,000) on a registered 10DLC number, inbound free. 7-day trial, no credit card. Always verify the live price.

answers.q: What is the catch with Kixie?
answers.a: Plan for 30-60% above the sticker: minutes, the multi-line dialer and AI human-voice-detection all bill separately, and the quarterly auto-renewing contract only allows downgrades in its final 30 days — read that clause before signing. The dialer itself is genuinely fast and CRM-native; just buy it with the full basket priced and the calendar reminder set (our Renewal Radar exists for exactly this).

Koongo is genuinely best for Shopify merchants selling across several European marketplaces — Bol, Zalando, Allegro, Cdiscount, Miinto and the rest — who need inventory and order sync to run automatically, and who have priced their own item, feed and order counts against the surcharge table rather than the headline. Skip it if you sell on one channel or need product feeds only, where the feed-manager-only form from $14.50 or a dedicated feed app is cheaper; or your catalogue and order volume sit far enough above the included limits that the surcharges, not the plan, become the price.

(read 2026-08-23 on apps.shopify.com/koongo, listed as “Koongo: Sell on Marketplaces”, and on koongo.com/pricing) Four tiers on the listing, separated by update frequency rather than by capability. Free covers one store language, 100 items or SKUs, 5 product feeds, one marketplace wizard and up to 10 orders a month, updating once a day. Lite is $39 a month and updates every 6 hours, Starter is $79 and updates every 30 minutes, and Pro is $119 and updates every 15 minutes. All three include 1,000 items, 5 feeds, two marketplace wizards with the second free on a summer promotion, and 100 orders a month. All three also carry a 7-day free trial. Every paid tier states surcharges for extras used — items, feeds, marketplaces and orders — and each is also sold in a feed-manager-only form, from $14.50 for Lite, $29 for Starter and $41 for Pro. All charges on the listing are billed in USD and recur every 30 days. The vendor's own pricing page sells the same four plans in euros at €0, €35, €69 and €99 a month, and states that all prices exclude VAT. Each plan is broken into Core, Marketplace Manager, Feed Manager and Ads Manager modules with separate prices. There is also a surcharge table for extra stores, items, orders, marketplaces, feeds and team seats, where an extra 100 orders runs from €10.00 down to €2.00 as volume grows. Developer Koongo, a product of NoStress Commerce s.r.o., Prague; the app launched on 5 November 2014 and had 98 reviews at a 4.4 average at the time of writing. Always verify the live price.

answers.q: What is the catch with Koongo?
answers.a:
The headline price is a base, not a bill. Each paid plan includes 1,000 items, 5 feeds, two marketplace wizards and 100 orders a month, and the listing says plainly that surcharges apply for extras used across all four of those dimensions. For a store with a real catalogue selling on several European marketplaces, every one of those limits is one you pass in week one. Price your own numbers on koongo.com's surcharge table before you take $39 seriously.

The two pricing pages also do not quote the same bill. The App Store lists $39, $79 and $119 and bills in USD. koongo.com lists €35, €69 and €99 and states that all prices exclude VAT. Depending on where you trade and how you are registered, those are meaningfully different amounts for the same plan, and nothing on either page reconciles them.

Then the record, which is the most useful thing on this listing. 4.4 from 98 reviews is the lowest average in this category among the apps Shopify shows beside it, and the breakdown explains why: 84 five-star ratings sit alongside six one-star ones. The critical reviews are specific rather than vague, which makes them worth reading in full. In July 2026 a Belgian merchant described a repricer set to Monitoring Mode that still blocked updates to live Bol offers because of MinimumPrice errors, so a delivery-promise change never reached the marketplace. In January 2026 a UK merchant described unresolved integration errors on OnBuy and a refused refund, with Koongo replying publicly that they had reached out several times without response. Neither is disqualifying on its own. Together they describe an app whose complexity is real and whose marketplace integrations sometimes need support to untangle — which is consistent with the vendor's own listing offering personal onboarding for complex setups.

One more line to read before you install: the listing states the app views sensitive customer data as well as device and activity data, and can view and edit products, orders and custom data. Marketplace order sync needs customer details to work, so that is expected, but it makes this a processor of personal data on your behalf rather than a feed formatter.

KrispCall is genuinely best for sales and support teams that need virtual numbers across many countries with a shared dashboard, dialer and CRM hooks at a budget seat price. Skip it if your calling is domestic-only at low volume (simpler tools suffice), or you need enterprise reliability guarantees over price.

(re-verified 2026-08-17 against the vendor's own pricing page) Essential $12 per user/mo billed annually or $15 monthly, for solo agents and teams up to 5 people; Standard $32 per user/mo annually or $40 monthly, for teams scaling up to 50 users; Enterprise custom. Annual saves 20%, which the page puts at $36 per user a year on Essential and $96 on Standard, and each plan comes with $1 of free calling and SMS credit. Calls and SMS are otherwise pay-as-you-go from a separate credit balance, and numbers carry their own one-off and monthly charges (from $4.50 one-off and $1.50 a month at the time of reading). Always verify the live price.

answers.q: What is the catch with KrispCall?
answers.a: Same honest math as most budget VoIP: the plan buys the platform, the meter buys the conversations — per-minute and per-SMS charges land on top of every seat, so the comparison that matters is call-rate-per-country at your volume. The 100+ country number coverage is genuinely the draw; verify number availability and local regulations for your specific target countries before committing.

Kumo is genuinely best for Shopify merchants on a standard plan who need wholesale prices for named customer groups, with CSV price lists and a registration form that someone approves, and who would rather not pay three times as much for a heavier wholesale app. Skip it if you are already on Shopify Plus, where company accounts and price lists come with the platform; or you want prices that react to competitors or to the market, because this sets fixed rules per customer group and nothing reads the outside world.

(read 2026-09-16 on apps.shopify.com/b2b-wholesale-tools) Two plans and no free tier: B2B at $15 a month and PLUS at $30, both with a 7-day free trial, billed in USD every 30 days. B2B carries the whole working app — wholesale pricing, volume pricing, customer registration forms and the approval workflow — and pricing rules are unlimited rather than metered, so the ladder is not a volume ladder. PLUS adds exactly three things, and all three are Shopify Plus features: company registration, product catalog assignment and checkout integration. If you are not on Shopify Plus, the $30 tier has nothing to sell you. The app is Built for Shopify, launched on 21 November 2024, and shows 5.0 stars over 9 reviews. Always verify the live price.

answers.q: What is the catch with Kumo?
answers.a:
Five stars over nine reviews is not a track record, and the age makes that worse rather than better. The app launched on 21 November 2024, so it has had close to two years on the App Store to collect them. Nine reviews in that window is a small installed base, and a small installed base is what decides whether an app is still maintained in 2028 — the rating tells you the nine are happy, not that the app is safe to build a wholesale channel on.

The second plan is a trap for anyone who reads the ladder as a feature ladder. PLUS costs twice B2B and the three things it adds — company registration, catalog assignment, checkout integration — are all labelled Shopify Plus on the listing itself. On a standard Shopify plan the extra $15 a month buys nothing you can switch on.

Landingi is genuinely best for budget-conscious teams, international businesses and anyone needing bulk or programmatic page generation across 29 languages. Skip it if you need AI traffic routing, real-time collaboration or deep technical control — that's where Unbounce earns its higher price.

(re-verified 2026-08-17; the English page quotes USD while the same page served from a Dutch address quotes euros at the same numerals, so check your own currency) Four plans, billed annually: Build $24/month, Optimize $119/month, Scale from $229/month and Enterprise from $1,199/month. Annual billing includes two months free against monthly. Custom domains are metered: 1 on Build, 3 on Optimize, 10 on Scale and 100 on Enterprise, with extras at $5 a month each. AI credits come with the plan (2,500, 10,000, 20,000 and 60,000 a month) and top-ups are pay-as-you-go at $15 for 5,000, $25 for 10,000 and $40 for 20,000. A promotional rate roughly half the Build price appears periodically — it is a limited-time offer rather than the standard rate. Always verify the live price.

answers.q: What is the catch with Landingi?
answers.a: You trade away the high-end optimisation: no AI traffic routing like Unbounce's Smart Traffic, no real-time collaboration, and thinner technical control (script containers). Excellent value, but not the conversion-optimisation powerhouse.

LangShop is genuinely best for Shopify merchants selling into several language markets who want machine translation they can correct by hand — glossary rules, brand terms, bulk editing — plus a geolocated language and currency switcher, and whose catalogue and language count fit inside a published tier. Skip it if you sell in one language; or your translations must land in metafields without checking, which is precisely what the recent one-star reviews say is unreliable; or your catalogue is large enough that the tier you need is one of the unlisted ones — check langshop.app/pricing rather than the Shopify listing before you budget.

(read 2026-09-10 on apps.shopify.com/langshop and langshop.app/pricing) Seven published tiers, billed in USD. The Shopify listing shows only the first four and links to 'more pricing plans'; the vendor's own pricing page prices the rest. Free costs nothing and covers one language and 50 products, with limited manual and AI translation, the standard language and currency switcher and multilingual SEO. Basic is $10 a month or $100 a year, and raises that to 250 products with five glossary rules, unlimited editing of translations, bulk editing and removal of LangShop branding. Standard is $40 a month or $400 a year: three languages, 2,000 products, 100 glossary rules, automatic sync of 50 new items, and the point at which the named engines (OpenAI, DeepL Pro, Google Cloud Translation), the advanced switcher and translation of dynamic content and third-party apps become available. Advanced is $75 a month or $750 a year: five languages, 5,000 products, 250 glossary rules, sync of 125 new items, ten content-exclusion rules and Shopify Flow support. Beyond the listing: Pro at $120 a month or $1,200 a year adds API access with ten languages, 10,000 products, 500 glossary rules, sync of 250 and 50 exclusion rules; Enterprise at $250 or $2,500 gives 20 languages, 50,000 products, 1,000 glossary rules, sync of 1,250, 200 exclusion rules and a customer success manager; Unlimited at $500 or $5,000 lifts products, glossary, sync and exclusion rules to unlimited at 20 languages. Annual billing is described as two months free, which is the same 17% the listing quotes. Trial length is inconsistent across the vendor's own pages: every plan card on langshop.app/pricing says 7-day, while langshop.app/faq and the Shopify listing both say 14-day. Always verify the live price.

answers.q: What is the catch with LangShop?
answers.a: Two things sit awkwardly next to each other in the plan table. The headline promise is 'unlimited words', but every tier caps how many products you may translate and how many languages you may run, so the meter you actually pay is catalogue size. And the named engines that the listing leads with — OpenAI, DeepL Pro, Google Cloud Translation — are a Standard-tier feature at $40 a month; below that you get limited manual and AI translation. The Shopify listing also understates the ladder: it stops at Advanced and links to 'more pricing plans', while the vendor's pricing page publishes Pro at $120, Enterprise at $250 and Unlimited at $500 — and API access, which no listing tier mentions, starts at Pro. The app is old enough to judge (launched 15 September 2016, developer Aheadworks) and most of its 480 reviews are positive, but 23 of them are one-star, and the recent negative ones are specific rather than vague: a Slovak store reporting that metafield translations ignore both the AI store context and the glossary rules, and a Swedish store of almost three years reporting that products duplicated from another product carry the wrong translation across. If metafields or duplicated products are central to your catalogue, test exactly that during the trial.

Later is genuinely best for creators and visual-first brands (Instagram/TikTok-centric) that want drag-and-drop visual planning, link-in-bio and scheduling in one. Skip it if you need deep multi-network publishing, listening and team workflows at agency scale (suite-class tools fit), or the post caps chafe immediately.

(re-verified 2026-08-17) Starter $18.75/month, Growth $37.50 and Scale $82.50, all billed yearly, which Later advertises as three months free and 25% off against monthly. Every plan opens with a 14-day trial, and on the page as we read it on 31 August 2026 that trial is the only no-cost route offered: three paid tiers, nothing beneath them, and an FAQ that discusses users per plan rather than any zero-price option. Our earlier note here also described a permanently free option, which we could not source; Later has historically run a no-cost link-in-bio product that may still sit behind the signup flow, but the pricing page does not sell it.
