Add-ons on every tier: listening across social, web and news from $75/mo, X (Twitter) $29/mo, Employee Advocacy free for 3 advocates then from $199/mo for 25. 14-day trial, no card. Always verify the live price.

answers.q: What is the catch with Vista Social?
answers.a: It undercuts the big suites convincingly. The honest check is coverage depth: platform APIs change constantly, so verify the specific networks and features YOUR clients need (particularly newer TikTok/threads capabilities and approval workflows) inside the trial rather than trusting the comparison table. Agencies stepping up from Professional hit the Scale tier for white-labeling — price that step into client contracts from day one.

Volza is genuinely best for import-export businesses and sourcing teams that want global customs-level trade data plus verified buyer/supplier contacts at a fraction of enterprise pricing. Skip it if you only need US shipment data with fast daily updates (ImportGenius refreshes daily), or you're not doing import/export — this is a niche intelligence tool.

(read 2026-09-01 on volza.com/pricing) Three paid annual plans and a free trial. Startup is $1,500 a year: 182 countries (44 export and 50 import detailed databases, 160 export and 158 import mirror databases, 7 export and 7 import one-side databases, premium countries excluded), data from 2014 onward, 6,000 searches, full shipment view, 360,000 full-shipment download credits and 2 users. SME is $4,500 a year: 200 countries, adds the statistical databases (46 export, 48 import), unlimited searches under fair use, 1,040,000 download credits and 10 users. Corporate is $9,600 a year: the same 200-country coverage, unlimited searches under fair use, 2,400,000 download credits and 15 users. The free trial runs 7 days with no card, is advertised as "$50 On sign up + Unlimited Volza credits", shows the last three years in full view with a six-month preview, and carries no full-shipment download credits. An annual and a 2-year value plan are offered as billing terms. The page also states a refund promise: if you find no profitable opportunity, Volza will help you find one or refund in full. Always verify the live price.

answers.q: What is the catch with Volza?
answers.a: Three honest catches. The entry plan is narrower than the marketing implies: $1,500 a year covers 182 countries and two users, while the 200-country coverage and ten seats start at $4,500. Downloads run on a credit allowance — 360,000 a year on Startup — and an earlier reading of the catalogue put the cost per record at one credit for US or India shipments and up to ten in thinner markets; that per-country rate is not stated on the current pricing page and we could not re-verify it on 1 September 2026, so treat it as a question for sales rather than a fact. And the update cycle is slow, with some datasets taking up to two months to refresh, which suits structural questions far better than reactive ones. There is a learning curve too; it rewards analysts, not casual users.

Voye is genuinely best for companies with regularly traveling teams that want one pooled global data contract, per-user controls and an end to roaming bill surprises. Skip it if travel is rare (per-trip consumer eSIMs are simpler), or your destinations are few enough for local SIM discipline.

Published plans (read 6 September 2026 on their plans page). Monthly, 30-day validity: $9.99 for 5 GB, $19.99 for 12 GB, $39.99 for 30 GB, $69.99 for 55 GB, $119.99 for 100 GB — $2.00 down to $1.20 per gigabyte. Yearly, a single payment, 365-day validity: $500 for 200 GB, $1,000 for 450 GB, $2,000 for 950 GB, $3,500 for 1,800 GB — $2.50 down to $1.94 per gigabyte. Three-month billing is exactly three times the monthly price, with no discount. Enterprise — unlimited eSIMs, priority support and onboarding — is quoted by their sales team. Always verify the live price.

answers.q: What is the catch with Voye?
answers.a: eSIM data pooling genuinely beats classic roaming for traveling teams, but the honest homework is coverage-and-speed on YOUR corridors: quality varies by country and local carrier partner, so pilot with two or three of your heaviest travelers before migrating everyone. And note the vendor-cited savings numbers are marketing math until your own invoice confirms them.

WP Rocket is genuinely best for WordPress owners who want near-instant page-speed gains out of the box without touching cache config. Skip it if you're comfortable configuring a free caching plugin like LiteSpeed Cache or W3 Total Cache and enjoy the tinkering.

answers.q: How much does WP Rocket cost?
answers.a: (re-verified 2026-09-14 on their own pricing page, which had not moved since our September reading: the same three licences at the same rates, the same 50/100/500 site-count selector on Multi, and all three tiers now carrying Rocket Insights at no extra cost) These are annual licences, and the page prices in the visitor's currency. Read from Europe it sets EUR and shows Single €49.95/yr (1 website), Plus €99.95/yr (3 websites) and Multi €249.95/yr, and the 95 cents matter because an earlier reading rounded all three down to whole euros. Multi carries a site-count selector at 50, 100 or 500 websites, and anything above 500 is a custom licence. The dollar storefront reads $59, $119 and $299 a year for the same three tiers. Our own pricing screenshot on this page is that USD version, captured 12 August 2026, so the figures beside it are the euro ones from the same day. The two are not a contradiction but two storefronts of the same product. All tiers are feature-identical — you pay for the number of sites. There is no trial; the page offers a 14-day refund instead, and the licence auto-renews after a year, switchable off in your account's Billing section. What the page does not say anywhere is what it renews at. Always verify the live price.

answers.q: What is the catch with WP Rocket?
answers.a: It's a subscription, not a lifetime license — you keep your settings if you stop paying but lose updates and support, and a technically-minded user can get most of the way there with a free caching plugin. Two things to check before you buy on price. The Multi licence is capped now: 50, 100 or 500 websites, with a custom licence above that, so there is no unlimited tier to grow into. And the renewal rate is not published — the page confirms the licence auto-renews after a year but never states at what price, which is exactly where the Trustpilot complaints cluster.

Warmup Inbox is genuinely best for outbound teams warming new sending domains and inboxes before campaigns, with integrations across Google, Outlook, Zoho and SendGrid. Skip it if you want to compare costs before creating an account — the public page will not let you — or your sending volume is too low to need dedicated warm-up.

answers.q: How much does Warmup Inbox cost?
answers.a: (re-read 2026-09-05 on warmupinbox.com/pricing, both billing toggles) Three tiers, priced per inbox. Billed monthly: Basic $19 an inbox a month for 75 warmup messages a day, Pro $59 for 250 a day, Max $99 for 1,000 a day. Billed yearly the same three read $15, $49 and $79 a month ($180, $588 and $948 a year), which is the 20% saving the page advertises. The tiers also differ on the reply rate to your warmup mail — up to 25% on Basic, 45% on Pro and 50% on Max — and Pro adds your own templates, chosen warmup topics, language warmup and scheduled warmup. There is a free trial with no credit card, and the vendor states more than 30,000 real inboxes in the network. Always verify the live price.

answers.q: What is the catch with Warmup Inbox?
answers.a: The pricing is published and readable — three tiers, per inbox, with both billing toggles printing a rate: $19, $59 and $99 monthly, or $15, $49 and $79 on the yearly plan. The bigger caveat is structural: warmup is priced per inbox, so a team running twenty sending addresses pays twenty times the headline. And warmup is a floor, not a ceiling — it builds sender reputation, but no amount of it rescues a bad list or a bad offer.

Warn is genuinely best for shopify merchants who know exactly which notice they need — a Prop 65 label, a shipping-delay alert, an age-verification disclaimer, a we-no-longer-ship-here message — and want it on the right products, collections or countries without touching theme code, for $6.99 a month or nothing at all if one plain warning will do. Skip it if you are on a standard Shopify plan and specifically want the checkout blocked or a warning shown on the Checkout page: both are Plus Plan features and the Plus Plan is for Shopify Plus stores, so the capability the app's name advertises is not available to you at any price here. Also skip it if you sell off Shopify, or if what you actually need is consent and privacy management — cookie banners, consent records, data-subject requests — rather than a notice on a page..

(prices read 2026-09-20 on apps.shopify.com/product-notes) Billed in USD, every 30 days, and the ladder has three steps rather than the two the app's own summary suggests. Free gives you one textual warning across unlimited products, with the styling, per-product targeting and per-country targeting included. Premium is $6.99 a month or $41.94 a year, and the annual figure really is half of twelve monthly payments. It lifts the cap to unlimited warnings, notes and pop-ups, adds cart and checkout warnings, targeting by product or collection, and US-state geo-targeting on top of country targeting — but the plan is labelled for all stores EXCEPT Shopify Plus. Plus Plan is $12.99 a month or $77.94 a year, again exactly half of twelve monthly payments, and it is the Shopify Plus plan: the same feature list, plus warnings shown on the Checkout itself and the rule that lets a warning block checkout when configured. Both paid plans carry a 7-day free trial. Always verify the live price.

answers.q: What is the catch with Warn?
answers.a:
The app is called Warn: Warnings Checkout Blocks, and blocking checkout is the one thing most readers of this listing cannot buy at the advertised price. Checkout blocking, and showing a warning on the Checkout page at all, sits on the Plus Plan at $12.99 a month — and that plan says, in the App Store's own words, that it is for Shopify Plus stores. The $6.99 Premium plan says the opposite: for all stores except Shopify Plus. So the two tiers are not a small ladder and a big one, they are two different audiences, and which one you may buy is decided by your Shopify subscription rather than by how much warning you need. If you are on a standard Shopify plan and came here to stop a checkout, read the plan labels before you install.

The second thing to be clear about is what the app does and does not take off your hands. It renders the notice, targets it by product, collection or country, and styles it to your store. It does not tell you what Proposition 65, a GDPR withdrawal notice or an age-verification disclaimer has to say in your jurisdiction, and it does not keep that wording current when the rule changes. The compliance language stays your problem and your liability; this is the display layer for it.

Wati is genuinely best for businesses that want to run WhatsApp support and broadcasts at scale with a shared team inbox and automation. Skip it if your customers aren't on WhatsApp or your volume is tiny — the platform fee plus per-message costs aren't worth it for a trickle.

(re-verified 2026-09-12, read on their own pricing page — which again served us euros, not dollars) Growth €59/mo, Pro €119/mo and Business €279/mo billed annually, or €69, €149 and €349 billed monthly, with a 7-day free trial and no setup fee. Users are capped per tier: Growth includes 3 and lets you add none at all; Pro and Business include 5, with extra seats at €39 and €89 per user per month. Add-ons are separate again — 1,000 automation triggers €35/mo, 1,000 AI co-pilot credits €25/mo, Shopify $4.99/mo, each extra WhatsApp number €29/mo — and the Astra AI agents, which the page describes as deployable to web, WhatsApp and voice, are an add-on priced separately. Our dollar reading of the same page on 23 July 2026 gave Growth $39, Pro $79 and Business $199 annually, so which currency and which figure you see depends on where Wati places you — check your own checkout. Always verify the live price.

answers.q: What is the catch with Wati?
answers.a: The plan price is the smallest part of the bill. Growth is capped at three users and you cannot buy a fourth at any price, so growing past three people forces the jump to Pro; from there extra seats are €39 each, and €89 each on Business, on the euro storefront we have been served since August (our July dollar reading of the same two lines was $24 and $69). Automation triggers, AI co-pilot credits, the Astra AI agents, the Shopify link and every additional WhatsApp number are all separately metered, and Meta's per-conversation fees land on top of the lot. Model your real message volume and seat count before committing — that is where the money actually goes.

Way is genuinely best for retailers and brands with physical stockists who want a Google Maps locator on their Shopify storefront without setting up a Maps API key or paying Google directly — the app handles the key on every tier, including the free one, which removes the developer step. Skip it if you have one shop and do not mind the app's branding under your map, because the free tier already covers you; or you need routing, appointment booking or stock-by-location, since this maps and directs and does not do any of that.

(re-verified 2026-09-19) Four tiers, and above the first one the ladder is a location counter rather than a feature list. Free carries one store location, the floating Google Maps locator, appearance customisation and online support, with the app's own branding shown on your storefront. Basic is $6.99 a month or $67.10 a year and removes that branding, raising the limit to 50 locations and adding the map widget as an app block, a pop-up modal for multiple locations, full customisation with custom CSS, and bulk import and export. Advanced at $14.99 a month or $143.90 a year and Pro at $29.99 or $287.90 list exactly the same eight features as Basic; what they add is headroom, 500 locations and 2,000. Annual billing saves a stated 20% on every paid tier and each carries a 7-day free trial. No Google Maps API key is required on any plan. Charges are in USD and recur every 30 days. One line in the feature bullets sits against all of that: it advertises unlimited store locations, which no plan card offers. Developer Effective Apps, Ashdod, Israel; the app launched 24 April 2020, carries Shopify's Built for Shopify badge, names eleven interface languages and works with Google Maps, Apple Maps, Mapbox and Shopify's B2B solution. The review record read 134 at 4.7 on 19 September 2026, up one from 16 September: 118 five-star, 11 four-star, none at three, 3 at two and 2 at one. Always verify the live price.

answers.q: What is the catch with Way?
answers.a:
The pricing page reads like a feature ladder and behaves like a counter. Basic, Advanced and Pro list the same eight capabilities, so the $8 and $23 steps above Basic buy nothing but a higher location limit, and the jump from 50 to 500 leaves no tier in between. A chain with 60 or 80 shops pays the 500-location price and uses a tenth of it.

The free plan is genuinely usable on a live store, which is worth saying plainly — the same developer's Blocky and TiXel listings advertise free plans that turn out to be development stores only, and this one is not that. What it does carry is the app's branding on your storefront and a hard limit of one location, so it is a real free tier for a single shop rather than a trial in disguise.

Weave is genuinely best for dental, optometry and small healthcare practices that want phone, texting, payments and reviews unified for the front desk. Skip it if you're outside healthcare/practice verticals, or you're a single small office where a simple VoIP line and a separate review tool cost far less.

Weave sells a per-location monthly subscription and its pricing page (weavehq.com/pricing, read 5 September 2026) now states plans start from $199 per location a month, though the exact tier ladder is still only shown after a demo. Practice owners commonly report all-in costs of roughly $400 to $700 a location once phones, payments and add-ons are bundled, plus a one-time setup fee of about $750. Quote-driven above the floor. Always verify the live price.

answers.q: What is the catch with Weave?
answers.a: Two honest cautions. The $199 starting price is a floor, not the bill: add-ons, setup and per-location fees land on top, and the full tier ladder is only shown in a demo, so get everything in writing. And it's deeply tuned for healthcare and appointment-based practices; a general small business will find much of the workflow assumes a front desk and a patient schedule.

WebCatalog is genuinely best for people juggling many web apps and multiple accounts per service who want them as clean, separate desktop apps with per-profile isolation. Skip it if browser tab discipline or built-in PWA installs already cover you, or you use a handful of apps with single accounts.

(read 2026-08-25 on their own pricing page, re-read 2026-09-10 in a browser) Basic is free and no card is required: 2 desktop apps, 2 profiles and 1 space. Pro is $5 per user per month billed annually, plus local taxes, and lifts those caps to unlimited apps, profiles and spaces with cloud sync, pages, theme colours, an ads and tracker blocker, an app lock and location services. Business is $8 per user per month billed annually and adds shared spaces, shared pages, team management, centralised billing and an activity log, with SAML single sign-on. Both paid plans carry a 7-day trial. The page prices in USD, EUR or JPY. A legacy lifetime licence is not mentioned on the pricing page or in the help docs (checked 2026-09-10). Always verify the live price.

answers.q: What is the catch with WebCatalog?
answers.a: It solves a real annoyance: dozens of web apps and multiple accounts per app as tidy desktop windows. The honest question is whether you need the paid tier at all. The free plan's 2-app limit is tight, but browser profiles and PWAs solve part of the same problem for free. Pro earns its fee when multi-account juggling (several Gmail/Slack/WhatsApp identities) is daily reality.

Webflow is genuinely best for designers and marketing teams who want to ship a real, fast site without a developer in the loop for every change, and who value that the CMS and hosting are the same product as the editor. Skip it if you are one person publishing a simple site. The free tier and a $15 site plan cover that, and the reason to be here is the team workflow you are not using. Also skip the entry ecommerce plan if you sell in any volume, because 2% of every order will outrun the $45 a month that Plus costs extra.

(re-verified 2026-08-04, read on their own pricing page with every plan accordion and billing tab open) Webflow bills in two places at once. Site plans, billed yearly: Starter free; $15/mo for a site that does not need a CMS (custom domain, 300 static pages, 10 GB bandwidth); $25/mo for the CMS tier, which the page now calls Premium. Ecommerce site plans are separate again: Standard $29/mo with 500 items and a 2% transaction fee, Plus $74/mo with 5,000 items and no transaction fee, Advanced $212/mo with 15,000 items. Workspace plans, also billed yearly: Starter free (2 staging sites, 1 full seat), Core $19/mo, Growth $49/mo, and on the freelancer-and-agency tab Freelancer $16/mo and Agency $35/mo. Seats are charged on top of the workspace plan: a full seat is $39/mo billed yearly, a limited seat $15/mo, a review-only seat $0. Platform plans start at Team $2,500/mo with an annual contract required, and Enterprise above it is quote-only. Add-ons: Optimize from $299/mo by page views, Analyze from $9/mo by sessions, Localize Essential $9/mo and Localize Advanced $29/mo by number of locales, 2,000 AI credits $20/mo billed yearly, and a published bandwidth ladder running from +50 GB at $20/mo billed annually to +2.45 TB at $974/mo, with monthly billing about half again as expensive at every step. Webflow Cloud overages run at $2 per million requests and $2 per 5 hours of CPU usage, with web app bandwidth pooled into the site plan's bandwidth. Storage is priced on that page again: on the Basic and CMS site plans the D1 and KV stores include 100 MB and then run at $2 per 500 MB, and R2 object storage at $2 per 5 GB; on the Team plan those same lines read $2 per GB. (Re-verified 2026-08-29 on the pricing page itself: every plan, seat and add-on price above was unchanged.) Always verify the live price.

answers.q: What is the catch with Webflow?
answers.a: Three separate bills, and the pricing page shows them on separate tabs. A site plan is what puts your site online: $15 a month for a static site, $25 with the CMS. A workspace plan is what lets your team work on it: $19 or $49 a month. And seats are charged on top of the workspace plan at $39 a month each for anyone who can actually design. So a two-person team on a CMS site is not $25 a month — it is $25 for the site, $19 for the workspace and $39 for the second seat, which is $83, and that is before add-ons. Two more numbers to find before you commit. The entry ecommerce plan takes a 2% transaction fee on every order, which the $29 headline does not mention and which is the largest single cost for anyone selling real volume; removing it means Plus at $74. And Optimize, the conversion tooling Webflow leads with in its marketing, starts at $299 a month on top of everything else and is priced by page views. Price your team, your site and your add-ons together, because no single tab on that page shows you a total.

WebinarGeek is genuinely best for marketing and sales teams running live and automated webinars in Europe who want a polished, GDPR-friendly platform with viewer-tier pricing. Skip it if you run occasional small webinars (your video-call tool may cover it), or you need the CRM and localization features that sit behind paid add-ons.

(re-verified 2026-09-14 on the vendor's own pricing page, read in EUR) The plans are Basic, Premium and Enterprise; an earlier reading of ours called the first two Premium and Advanced, which was wrong. Basic is €69/mo, or €49 billed annually, and covers 50 viewers, 1 presenter and a 2-hour session. Premium is bought per viewer tier: €99/€69 at 125 viewers, €159/€99 at 250, €249/€139 at 500 and €399/€199 at 1,000 (monthly/annual). The annual discount widens as you climb, from 30% at 125 viewers to the advertised 50% at 1,000, so "save up to 50%" only holds on the top rung. Enterprise is annual-only and quoted from €349 at 500 viewers, €449 at 1,000, €649 at 2,000 and €849 at 5,000. The page carries a currency switch across EUR, USD, GBP, SEK, NOK and DKK and serves by region, so both the number and the currency depend on where you buy; the figures render client-side and a plain fetch retrieves none of them. Add-ons are billed annually on top of a Premium subscription: extra users from €10 per user per month, localisation €20, AI assistant €20, branding profiles €59 (which include an extra workspace and e-mail domain), HubSpot €49, Salesforce €49 and RTMP streaming €34.50, plus a one-off €495 for online onboarding. Always verify the live price.

answers.q: What is the catch with WebinarGeek?
answers.a: The friendly €49 headline is the annual rate for just 50 viewers, and the real cost lives in add-ons: localisation, the AI assistant, CRM integrations, RTMP and branding profiles are each €20-59 a month on top, and only a Premium subscription can buy them. A serious webinar stack quickly doubles the base plan.

Wegic is genuinely best for non-technical founders who want an AI to build and host a simple site fast, and are comfortable with usage-based credit pricing. Skip it if you want predictable flat pricing, or you'll iterate heavily — credits make redesigns expensive, and real use needs a paid plan quickly.

(re-verified 19 September 2026 on wegic.ai/pricing in a browser; the monthly headline figures stand on the 30 August reading from a US exit, see below) Credit-based AI website builder, priced in US dollars. Free: 100 credits at signup only, which Wegic's FAQ describes as credits to chat with the AI — generating a site is a paid action. Trial pack $2.99. Starter $39.90/month, or $286.80 a year — $23.90/month, the advertised 40% off — for 600 credits/mo (~$0.04/credit), a permanent .wegic.net address, code export, e-commerce product display, website analytics and removal of the Wegic watermark. Premium $69.90/month, or $502.80 a year ($41.90/month), for 2,000 credits/mo (~$0.02/credit), a custom domain and up to 70% off extra credit purchases. Wegic's own Stripe catalogue also carries two- and three-year terms that the plan table does not show: Starter $525.60 and $680.40, Premium $885.60 and $1,220.40. A separate Wegic Cloud balance for AI image and video generation runs on top: $20/month of credit on Starter, $35 on Premium. Credits do not roll over — at the end of each monthly billing cycle the remaining balance is cleared — and when a subscription ends published sites stay live for up to 7 more days, the Wegic badge returns, and a site on a custom domain is unpublished until you republish it on a Wegic address. On 19 September the annual totals, the credit allowances, the Cloud balances and the 40% annual discount all re-read unchanged; the two monthly headline figures are drawn as an animated digit strip that carries no readable text, so those rest on the August reading and on the annual totals, which match them. Always verify the live price.

answers.q: What is the catch with Wegic?
answers.a: Everything is credits, and generating a site burns them fast — Wegic's own page notes a single generation can cost over $10 in credits, while the free plan gives 100 credits once. The cheaper per-credit rate only kicks in on the higher annual tier, and premium AI media draws down a second 'Cloud' balance on top of your plan.

WhatConverts is genuinely best for agencies and lead-gen businesses that want every lead — calls, forms, chats — attributed to its source and campaign without enterprise-suite prices. Skip it if your leads flow through one channel (lighter tracking suffices), or nobody will act on the attribution data monthly.

(re-verified 2026-09-05 on whatconverts.com/pricing) Two ladders behind one toggle, and the page opens on the single-account one. Single account: Call Tracking $30 a month, Plus $60 (forms, chat, ecommerce), Pro $100 (HIPAA, call flows, report builder), Elite $160 (customer journey, multi-click attribution) — each including $30 of monthly usage credit. Agency, on the second tab, is three plans rather than one, all with unlimited accounts: Plus $500 a month with $250 of credit, Pro $800 with $300, Elite $1,250 with $400. Every tier carries a 14-day free trial. Past the included credit, the comparison table on the same page prints the usage rates: additional local numbers $2.50 each, local minutes 4.5 cents each, toll-free numbers $3.50 each, toll-free minutes 6.5 cents each, and white label $50 a month on every tier; call transcription is $0.02 and PCI redaction is priced separately. The billing FAQ adds that minutes are rounded up to the full minute and that a busy or no-answer call still counts once it connected to the tracking number. Always verify the live price.

answers.q: What is the catch with WhatConverts?
answers.a: The meter is honest and the unit rate is invisible: every phone number, call minute, text, form, chat, appointment, email, event and transaction is charged against a monthly credit, and past that credit WhatConverts publishes no unit price anywhere on its site — the billing FAQ points to a Rates page inside the account. You can still model the bill, just not check the arithmetic: the calculator on the pricing page turns a monthly volume into a usage figure, and on 10 September 2026 it put the $30 Call Tracking plan at no extra usage for 50 calls and 100 forms, $47 at 500 of each and $250 at 2,000 of each. Its genuine strength versus bigger attribution suites is capturing EVERY lead type (not just calls) at a fair price; the flip side is you still need someone to read the reports and reallocate budget, or it's measurement theater.

Wholesale Gorilla is genuinely best for Shopify merchants who already have wholesale buyers and want them ordering from the same store as retail customers — custom price groups, a signup and approval flow, net terms and wholesale-only shipping rules — without moving up to Shopify Plus for native B2B.. Skip it if you need one flat wholesale percentage and nothing else, which customer tags and a far cheaper app already cover; you are on Shopify Plus, where native B2B gives you price lists and payment terms without a second subscription; or you want volume-break pricing on a small budget, because that single feature costs $149.95 a month here..

answers.q: How much does Wholesale Gorilla cost?
answers.a: (read 2026-09-08 and re-read 2026-09-19 on apps.shopify.com/wholesale-gorilla and checked against the vendor's own plan-comparison page at wholesalegorilla.com/plan-comparison/, which lists the same three figures) Three tiers, all billed in USD every 30 days: Lite $34.95 a month, Advanced $69.95 and Premium $149.95. There is no free plan. Every tier carries a 21-day free trial and nothing beyond it, so budget from day 22. Nothing here is metered — pricing rules and customer price groups are unlimited on all three tiers — so what you are buying as you climb is features, not volume. The app has been on the Shopify App Store since 26 September 2018 and on 19 September 2026 showed 4.8 stars over 317 reviews — 275 five-star, 17 four, 8 three, 5 two and 12 one — up from 4.7 over 313 eleven days earlier. Its Works with field names only Checkout, customer accounts and Shopify Admin. Always verify the live price.

answers.q: What is the catch with Wholesale Gorilla?
answers.a: It is a feature ladder, not a volume ladder, and the features most people picture when they say wholesale sit high on it. Volume discounts — buy ten, pay less each — are Premium only, at $149.95 a month, more than four times the entry price. Discount codes, net payment terms, wholesale shipping rules and theme integration all start at Advanced, $69.95. Lite at $34.95 buys custom prices per customer group and a basic signup form, which is a price list rather than a wholesale channel. Work out which rung you actually need before you read $34.95 as your price, because the honest entry point for most wholesale operations is the middle one.

Wing Assistant is genuinely best for founders drowning in delegatable admin who have processes to hand off and want a managed VA without recruiting one themselves. Skip it if your workflows live only in your head — document or automate the repetitive work first, before paying a human to run undefined chaos.

answers.q: How much does Wing Assistant cost?
answers.a: (re-verified 2026-08-17 against Wing's own machine-readable pricing page) This is a managed assistant service, not software. General Virtual Assistant part-time is $699 a month and full-time $999 a month, which Wing presents as a 16% saving against the part-time rate pro-rated. Specialist roles are priced separately and enterprise is custom. The published package includes a dedicated assistant, a success manager and free replacement if the fit is wrong. Always verify the live price.

answers.q: What is the catch with Wing Assistant?
answers.a: You're renting a person, not automating a task — a good VA is real leverage, but only if you already have documented, delegatable work. Hand over chaos and you'll get chaos back, faster.

Wistia is genuinely best for marketing teams who want video on their own site with real analytics and lead capture, and who care that the player does not recommend a competitor's video afterwards. Skip it if you just need somewhere to put videos — an unlisted upload to a free platform does that, and the reason to pay here is the analytics and the branding control, not the hosting.

(re-verified 2026-09-19 on wistia.com/pricing, Video Platform tab; the monthly rates below were read with the page's billing toggle set to Monthly) Four tiers, and the headline numbers are the ANNUAL rates: the billing toggle on the page is set to Annual with a “Save 20%” chip, so Business at $79 a month and Business + Lead gen at $329 a month are what you pay when you commit for a year. Switch that toggle to Monthly and the same three cards read $0, $99 and $412 a month, with the per-extra-user rate moving from $25 to $31 — so the 20% the chip promises is real, and paying month to month costs about a fifth more. Those monthly figures are rendered by the page rather than written in its source, which is why they can only be read with a browser. Free $0: 25 GB storage, 1 user, 200 GB bandwidth, basic analytics, Wistia branding on the player. Business $79: 250 GB+ storage, 3 users, 1 TB bandwidth, branding removed, collections and playlists, in-video CTAs and forms, advanced analytics. Business + Lead gen $329 is Business plus the Automation Suite — marketing-platform connection (HubSpot, Adobe Marketo Engage, Pardot), lead capture and scoring, pipeline measurement — and the FAQ describes that suite as something you add to a Business plan rather than a separate product. Enterprise is quote-only: from 1 TB storage, 2 TB bandwidth, custom users, unlimited view-only access, team accounts, SSO, video playback protection, a dedicated customer success manager. Price per additional user $25. Three rows in the feature table carry a “$” instead of a tick in every column, Enterprise included: Webinars, AI audio descriptions, and video dubbing with lip syncing. The overage rules sit in the FAQ rather than on the cards. Bandwidth is included with every plan and resets every month; free accounts cannot exceed their limit, while paid plans are billed for usage beyond what is included or prepaid. Storage works the same way and can be bought upfront to avoid usage charges. Users are billed for usage beyond the seats the plan includes, as you add and remove them. Webinar and live-event allowances are per event and not cumulative across events; additional attendees are charged at $0.20 each and additional duration minutes at $2.00 each, billed on the next monthly billing date. You can cancel at any time unless you are on Enterprise or a signed order form, either at the end of the billing cycle or immediately, and no refund is issued either way. Webinar plans have their own tab on the same page and carry no price in the source. Always verify the live price.

answers.q: What is the catch with Wistia?
answers.a: Bandwidth is the meter that decides your bill, and it is the one number you cannot predict before you publish. A single video that does well can move you from Free to Business in a month, which is arguably the product working — but budget for it rather than being surprised. Their FAQ is precise about which way it cuts: free accounts cannot exceed their bandwidth limit, while paid plans are billed for usage beyond what is included or prepaid. The free tier carries Wistia branding on the player, so it is a trial with no time limit rather than a plan you can ship a brand on. The published prices are the annual ones; the page's toggle sits on Annual with a 20% saving and the month-to-month figures are not in its source, so a monthly subscriber cannot price the plan from the pricing page. The webinar overages are the sharpest edge: $2.00 per extra minute means a session that runs long costs real money, the allowance is per event rather than cumulative, and both facts are in the FAQ rather than on the pricing card.

answers.q: Is Wiz Checkout Upsell worth it?
answers.a: Wiz Checkout Upsell is genuinely best for shopify merchants who want checkout-stage upsells, banners, trust badges and gift messages alongside post-purchase and thank-you page offers from a single app, and whose order volume already makes $99 a month a rounding error. Skip it if you were budgeting the $49 tier and expected checkout upsells with it — that plan is post-purchase only — or you want to test the idea at no cost first, because there is no free plan here.

answers.q: How much does Wiz Checkout Upsell cost?
answers.a: (prices re-verified 2026-09-19 on apps.shopify.com/checkout-pro; the ladder is unchanged since 2 September, one promotion is new) Three tiers, billed in USD every 30 days, each with a 14-day free trial and no free plan. Essential is $49 a month and covers post-purchase upsell funnels, thank-you page upsells and customization, order status page upsells and a review block, and all shipping and payment customizations; the listing marks that tier as not applicable for Shopify Plus. Plus Growth is $99 a month, or $999 a year (the listing says that saves 16%), and is the tier that opens the checkout itself: checkout upsells, subscription upgrades, checkout banners, reviews and trust badges, checkout input fields and gift messages, a checkout discount list and free gifts, on top of everything in Essential. That card now also carries a BFCM offer — "Pay only $1 for first month!" — with no end date printed beside it. Checkout concierge is $199 a month or $1,999 a year (save 16%) and adds custom onboarding and launch, A/B testing and analysis across all extensions, monthly performance review calls and custom extension development. Always verify the live price.

answers.q: What is the catch with Wiz Checkout Upsell?
answers.a: The name says checkout, but the $49 Essential plan does not include checkout upsells. That tier is post-purchase, thank-you page and order status page only, and the listing explicitly marks it as not applicable for Shopify Plus. Everything the app is named after — checkout upsells, checkout banners and trust badges, input fields, gift messages, free gifts at checkout — starts on the $99 Plus Growth plan. There is no free plan either, only a 14-day trial; as of 19 September that tier carries a BFCM offer of $1 for the first month, undated, so today the cheapest honest look at checkout upsells is a dollar and after this promotion it is $99 a month again. And A/B testing across all extensions, the feature you would want precisely to prove that $99 was worth it, sits one rung higher again at $199 — even though the listing advertises built-in A/B testing in its own highlights.

Woodpecker is genuinely best for outbound teams that want usage-priced cold email plus LinkedIn outreach, with unlimited seats and email accounts included instead of per-user fees. Skip it if you send occasional one-off campaigns (usage pricing only wins when you actually use it), or your motion is LinkedIn-heavy — $29 per connected account adds up.

(price re-verified 2026-09-18 against woodpecker.co/pricing) Free trial. Usage-priced: $7.00 per 100 contacted prospects, and the smallest volume the slider offers is 500 — so $35 a month is the practical entry rather than the $7 headline. Contact 200 prospects and you still pay $35; the per-100 figure only starts describing your bill once you are past that minimum. Unlimited team members and unlimited connected email accounts are included, and the page prices in twelve currencies (EUR, USD, GBP, CHF, AUD, BRL, CAD, DKK, INR, NOK, PLN, SEK). An annual toggle advertises SAVE 33% against monthly.

The sending allowance is derived, not chosen: the page states that emails per month equal contacted prospects multiplied by 16, the maximum number of campaign steps, which puts the 500-prospect entry at 16,000 emails a month. Add-ons are where an outbound motion actually gets expensive, and there are now two grades of managed sending address rather than one: LinkedIn accounts $29 a month each; email addresses on Google or Microsoft $6 a month each; email addresses on Maildoso, Mailforge, Infraforge or Azure $4 a month each; extra warm-ups $5 a month per email account; new domains at roughly $1 a month per domain, billed annually, which the page flags as an approximation because it depends on the domain name and shows the exact price before payment. Lead Finder credits start at 500 for $10. Always verify the live price.

answers.q: What is the catch with Woodpecker?
answers.a: The $7-per-100-prospects unit reads cheap, but a real outbound motion stacks add-ons fast. Every connected LinkedIn account is $29 a month, managed sending addresses $6 a month apiece and extra warm-ups $5 per account — and contacted prospects are the meter, so scaling outreach scales the bill.

answers.q: Is World Businesses for Sale worth it?
answers.a: World Businesses for Sale is genuinely best for owners selling established, often brick-and-mortar businesses — restaurants, shops, services, small manufacturers — who want international buyer exposure with hands-on guidance. Skip it if you're selling a small online asset (an auction-style online-business marketplace fits better), or you want a free listing — even the cheapest no-commission plan here costs £49 for 30 days.

answers.q: How much does World Businesses for Sale cost?
answers.a: (2026, re-verified 2026-09-10 on their own selling pages) Browsing is free for buyers. Sellers pick one of two tracks. Broker plans: Basic £395 (3% commission, 6-month contract), Standard £749 (2% commission, 9 months), Premium £1,500 (1% commission, 12-month contract, stays live until sold with free renewals) — every tier states commission is due only if they introduce the buyer. Or no-commission pay-as-you-go listings (inc. VAT): Basic £49, Standard £75 or Premium £99 for 30-day access. Take 10% off on a flex monthly subscription (£44.10 / £67.50 / £89.10) or 20% off on a 6-month plan (£235.20 / £360.00 / £475.20), and you keep 100% of the sale price. Free 24/7 chat guidance before you commit. Always verify the live price.

answers.q: What is the catch with World Businesses for Sale?
answers.a: On the broker plans you pay twice: a listing fee up front AND commission when it sells — 3% on Basic, 2% on Standard, 1% on Premium — on contracts of 6, 9 and 12 months. Only Premium stays live until sold with free renewals, so on the lower tiers a business that has not sold needs a paid renewal, and for a slow sale £1,500 once can beat £749 twice. Every tier says commission is payable only when they introduce the buyer, which is exactly the clause to read in the contract before you sign. If you want no commission at all, the pay-as-you-go plans start at £49 for 30 days — far cheaper up front, but those are listings, not broker introductions. As with any marketplace, the fee buys exposure, not a guaranteed sale.

Wrike is genuinely best for mid-to-large teams running complex, cross-functional projects that need robust reporting, workflows and resource management. Skip it if you're a small team that just wants a simple kanban board — a lighter tool is faster to adopt and cheaper.

(price re-verified 2026-09-05) A permanent free plan at $0 per user, with no user cap named on the plan card; Team $10 per user a month for 2 to 15 users; Business $25 per user a month for 5 to 200 users. Pinnacle and Apex publish no amount at all — both carry only a Contact us button and the line "Connect with us for pricing". Business and every tier above it is sold as an annual subscription only. Seats are bought in blocks: groups of five up to 30 seats, groups of 10 from 30 to 100, groups of 25 above 100. Self-service checkout covers Team and Business up to 15 users with no add-ons; beyond that the purchase goes through a Wrike representative. All prices are listed in US dollars and exclude local taxes. Always verify the live price.

answers.q: What is the catch with Wrike?
answers.a: It's powerful and scales to complex, cross-team portfolios, but that power brings a learning curve and a per-seat cost that climbs — small teams often find it heavier than they need next to a simpler board tool.

Xero is genuinely best for small businesses whose bookkeeper or accountant already works in Xero — the ecosystem and the bank feeds are the real product, and the monthly price is small against what the reconciliation time costs. Skip it if you invoice a handful of clients and reconcile by hand — the entry tier at $25 after the promo is buying automation you may not need yet, and simpler invoicing tools cost less.

(re-verified 2026-09-19 on their own US pricing page) Every headline price is still a promotion: 'Get 90% off your plan for your first 6 months when you buy by 30 September 2026'. Early is $2.50 a month for the first six months and then $25. Growing is $5.50 and then $55. Established is $9 and then $90. New on this reading: the same page carries a notice that Xero subscription prices are increasing from 1 October 2026 — the day after the offer closes — and does not print the new rates. Also new: the tier limits. Early is capped at 20 invoices and 5 bills a month, and the footnote states the invoice limit counts both approving and sending, and that transactions initiated by app partners may automatically contribute to it. Multi-currency and project tracking remain on Established only. The offer terms restrict it to new US customers buying their first organisation with code DC90626308US, cover the base subscription only, and auto-renew monthly at the regular price. Optional add-ons: Inventory Plus (no price shown, and excluded on Early) and Xero Payroll powered by Gusto at $36 a month plus $6 per employee or contractor, which the discount does not cover. Standard ACH bill payments are included; fees apply for other methods, same-day ACH and cross-border. Prices are USD and exclude tax; a downgrade is only allowed one month after an upgrade. Xero prices differently by country. Always verify the live price.

answers.q: What is the catch with Xero?
answers.a: Read the second number, not the first. Every plan on that page is 90% off for six months, and the price that governs the rest of your first year is ten times what the button says: $25, $55 and $90. That is not hidden — it is printed right there — but it is printed smaller, and the plan people pick on the strength of $2.50 a month is the one that becomes $25. Then read the notice further down, because it undercuts even that: Xero says subscription prices are increasing from 1 October 2026, the day after the offer closes, without printing the new rates. So month seven costs $25 or more, and the page will not tell you which. The second thing to check is the entry tier's ceiling: Early is 20 invoices and 5 bills a month, the limit counts approving as well as sending, and connected apps can eat into it on your behalf — which makes Growing at $55 the realistic starting price for anyone billing through other software. And check which country's page you are on, because Xero's tiers and prices differ by market.

Zedonk is genuinely best for small and mid-size fashion brands that need sales, production, inventory and wholesale in one system built around size curves, seasons and linesheets. Skip it if you are not a fashion business — this is deliberately niche — or you want self-serve, monthly-cancellable software rather than an annual, demo-led ERP.

(price re-verified 2026-09-09 against zedonk.co.uk/pricing; unchanged since our August reading) Modular fashion-ERP, priced per building block and billed annually, all listed as 'prices starting from': PLM £166/mo, ERP Essential £166/mo, B2C £250/mo and B2B £332/mo. The two upper cards read 'All ERP Essential Features PLUS' — Shopify integration and barcode generation on B2C, the B2B digital showroom on B2B — so those tiers contain the ERP rather than sitting on top of it. No self-serve signup: every tier goes through a demo, and the FAQ states the displayed plans are 'merely examples' and that a plan can be changed at any time. Onboarding and training are included in every plan; the FAQ puts implementation cost (customisation, data migration, integrations) in a separate figure quoted in a consultation. Always verify the live price.

answers.q: What is the catch with Zedonk?
answers.a: The 'starting from' wording is doing real work: £166/mo is the floor of the cheapest module, billed annually, so a working setup for a brand that sells wholesale quickly stacks toward £332/mo and beyond — about £4,000 a year before add-ons. There is no trial and no public total: you find out your actual price in a demo call. Budget for the stack, not the sticker.

Zeffy is genuinely best for small and mid-size nonprofits that want donations, ticketing, memberships and payments without any fee eating the mission's money. Skip it if your organization objects to donor-facing tip prompts on principle, or you need enterprise CRM-grade donor management built in.

(re-verified 2026-09-09 on zeffy.com/home/free-online-fundraising-platform) Still genuinely $0 for nonprofits: no platform fee, no transaction fee and no card-processing fee on donations, ticketing, shops, raffles, auctions, peer-to-peer or memberships. Zeffy states it covers transaction and credit-card fees itself and earns only from the optional tip donors are offered at checkout. Their own scale claim on that page: 100,000 nonprofits have raised $2B on Zeffy over seven years without paying a fee. Always verify the live price.

answers.q: What is the catch with Zeffy?
answers.a: The honest scrutiny of 'free': the tip prompt is shown to YOUR donors, with suggested percentages. Most give happily, but some organizations feel it inserts a step between donor and cause — and a donor who tips 10% effectively paid a fee, just voluntarily and not from your share. Compare that trade against the 2-5% the paid platforms take from every donation, and for most small nonprofits the math strongly favors Zeffy.

ZenBusiness is genuinely best for first-time founders who want the paperwork handled and are willing to pay a yearly fee to keep it handled — the a-la-carte pricing means you can start at the state fee plus a registered agent and add only what you actually need. Skip it if you are comfortable filing with your state yourself and acting as your own registered agent. In that case the state fee is the only unavoidable cost, and the $199/year is buying convenience and a business address rather than anything you cannot do. Also skip it if you need legal advice rather than filing, since a formation service is not a law firm.

(re-verified 2026-08-27 on their own pricing page; unchanged since 25 Jul 2026) Formation itself is $0 plus the state's fee — that applies to LLC, S corp and C corp filings alike, and the state fee is separate, varies by state and is not shown until you pick one. Everything else is priced as its own line rather than bundled into plan tiers. The recurring items are registered agent at $199/year, Worry-Free Compliance Filing at $199/year, and Advanced Compliance Protection at $299/year. One-time filings: operating agreement $99, EIN $99, business document templates $99, rush filing $79 and DBA registration $95 plus state fees. Then business licence report $149, amendment $100, certificate of good standing $100, annual report filing $100 per report, and New York publication $200 for the state that requires it. There is a second catalogue alongside the legal one: business website $129/year, eCommerce website $279/year, business email address $25/year, domain $25/year, domain privacy $10/year, logo kit $60, business banking $5/month and Money Pro with online payments $30/month. Always verify the live price.

answers.q: What is the catch with ZenBusiness?
answers.a: The $0 is real for the filing service and it is also the whole commercial idea: what you sign up for at zero has an annual carry that is not shown next to it. A registered agent is a legal requirement in every state, and theirs is $199/year — so the realistic first-year cost of 'the $0 LLC' is the state fee plus $199, before compliance filing at another $199/year. Price the second year, not the first. The second thing to hold in view is that the state fee is the largest and most variable number in the whole exercise, and ZenBusiness cannot change it. It is set by your state, ranges widely, and their own page sends you to a lookup rather than quoting it. Anyone comparing formation services on the advertised price alone is comparing the small half of the bill.

ZenZap is genuinely best for small teams that run work over messy WhatsApp/personal chat today and want organized, professional chat with tasks — starting free. Skip it if your workflows depend on a deep integration ecosystem (Slack's moat), or you're already paid into Microsoft Teams via 365.

(price re-verified 2026-09-01 against the vendor's own pricing page) (2026) Free plan: unlimited group chats, unlimited built-in to-dos, WhatsApp chat migration, AI voice-note transcription and in-chat search, 1 GB storage — the page publishes no user cap for it and no promise of unlimited seats. Pro $3/user/mo billed yearly ($4 monthly); Business+ $8/user yearly ($10 monthly); Enterprise custom. Flat-rate team bundles price below per-seat: Pro is $51/mo yearly for up to 20 users and $112 for up to 50, Business+ $89 and $190, quoted in dollars and pounds. Yearly billing saves 33%. Integrations with business tools and API access start at Business+; audit logs, SSO and SAML/SCIM are Enterprise. Always verify the live price.

answers.q: What is the catch with ZenZap?
answers.a: The pricing genuinely undercuts Slack — the honest question is ecosystem: team chat lives or dies on integrations and habit, and ZenZap's app catalog is a fraction of Slack's, so teams glued to hundreds of integrations will feel the gap. For WhatsApp-refugee teams that mainly need organized channels, tasks and work/life separation, the free tier is a remarkably complete landing spot.

Zendesk is genuinely best for support teams past the point where a shared inbox works, who need routing, a help centre and reporting in one place and have the volume to justify per-agent pricing. Skip it if you are a small team handling support out of email. The entry tier is email and ticketing only, the features people buy Zendesk for start at $55 a seat, and the Copilot AI is not available below $115. Also skip it if your case volume is low enough that per-resolution AI metering is more admin than benefit.

(re-verified 2026-08-12, read on their own pricing page from two countries) Per agent per month on annual billing, US storefront: Support Team $19, Suite Team $55, Suite Professional $115. Suite Enterprise + Copilot is quote-only. The page geo-prices — read from Europe the same three tiers show €19, €55 and €115 — so check which storefront your quote came from. Annual billing carries a stated 20% discount and the monthly rate is never printed. Paid add-ons on top of the seat price: Copilot $50 per agent/month (€50), Workforce Engagement bundle $50 (€50), Contact Center $83 (€82). Copilot can be attached to Professional and higher only. AI agents are included in Suite and Support plans but metered by 'automated resolutions' beyond the plan allowance, and App Builder, Action Builder and Voice are billed on consumption above their own allowances. Always verify the live price.

answers.q: What is the catch with Zendesk?
answers.a: Three separate multipliers sit on top of the number you first see. The prices shown are annual-billed — the page states a 20% annual discount and never prints the monthly rate, so budgeting month-to-month means adding roughly a quarter yourself. Copilot, the AI the product is currently sold on, is a $50 per-agent add-on that their own page restricts to Professional and higher: the $19 and $55 tiers cannot have it at any price, and on the $115 Professional seat it is a 43% uplift. And the AI agents that are included are metered by automated resolutions: past the allowance you pay per resolution, so the bill moves with how well the AI works rather than with how many people you hire. App Builder, Action Builder and Voice are metered on consumption alongside it. Price the tier you need with the add-ons you actually want switched on, because the $19 entry and a working configuration are far apart.

Zendrop is genuinely best for Shopify merchants starting or scaling a dropshipping or print-on-demand store who want sourcing, automated fulfilment, tracking and custom branding in one app, and who can price the per-order product and shipping cost into their margins. Skip it if you already have supplier relationships worth keeping, or you need the cheapest possible international shipping — the vetted US supplier network is the selling point here and you pay for it.

(re-read 2026-09-18 on apps.shopify.com/zendrop and on zendrop.com/pricing — the two do not carry the same ladder) On the Shopify listing: free to install, with three paid tiers, Beginner $29, Pro $49 and Plus $79 a month. What separates them is not features but how many products you may link to your store. The free tier allows none at all (“No linked products allowed”), Beginner covers 1-20, Pro 21-100 and Plus 101 or more; the feature list on all three paid tiers is identical (trending products, Zendrop Academy, Zendrop AI access, custom branding). Product and shipping cost is charged per order on top of every plan, and the listing states that external charges may be billed by Zendrop separately from your Shopify invoice. All charges are billed in USD and recur every 30 days. Rating 4.6 from 1,258 App Store reviews, up from 4.5 from 1,191 on 19 August 2026; the spread is 83% five-star (1.0K), 7% four-star (92), 2% three-star (19), 1% two-star (15) and 7% one-star (84). The listing does not carry Shopify's “Built for Shopify” badge. Developer Zendrop, 5499 North Federal Highway, Suite R, Boca Raton, FL, 33487, US; the app launched 4 November 2020. On zendrop.com/pricing the ladder is different: Free $0, Pro $49 a month or $399 a year, and Plus $79 a month or $549 a year, marked Most Popular. There is no $29 Beginner tier on their own site, and the annual rates appear only there — $399 is $33.25 a month and $549 is $45.75. The Summer Promo recorded here on 19 August 2026 (65% off annual Plus for the first year, advertised as a $357 saving, plus $100 in order credits, ending 31 August 2026) is gone: the page carries no percentage-off offer at all on 18 September 2026. Their own site also lists products the App Store listing does not mention, including AI-Built Stores, an AI Ad Generator and an MCP Server for connecting AI agents to a store. Always verify the live price.

answers.q: What is the catch with Zendrop?
answers.a: The free plan is a catalogue browser rather than a working tier: it allows no linked products, so nothing can actually be sold through it. Past that you are paying for an allowance, not for capability — Beginner, Pro and Plus carry exactly the same feature list, and the only thing $79 buys over $29 is room for more than a hundred linked products. The subscription is also the smaller half of the bill: product and shipping cost lands per order on top, and Zendrop bills that separately from your Shopify invoice, so the figure you budget is not the figure you pay. Their own pricing page and the App Store listing do not agree: the site sells Free, Pro and Plus with annual rates and no $29 tier, which means the price depends on where you sign up. And the 4.6 average covers a split verdict, with 83% five stars alongside 7% one star across 1,258 reviews — 84 people rating it bottom of the scale.

ZoomInfo is genuinely best for enterprise go-to-market teams that need the deepest US database, buyer-intent signals and conversation intelligence — and can absorb the contract. Skip it if you're an SMB or want flexible month-to-month pricing — the cost, credit burn and lock-in rarely pay off below enterprise scale.

Sales-gated, and re-verified as such on 2026-08-17: no public rates, no monthly billing and no free plan, with the pricing URL refusing plain requests and neither of our monthly captures retrieving a figure. Contracts typically start around $15k and the median runs near $32k a year, climbing once seats, credits and add-ons (intent data, international coverage) stack up — but those are third-party figures, not ZoomInfo's, and every deal is negotiated annually. Expect a multi-year push and price the credits, not just the seats. Always verify the live price.

answers.q: What is the catch with ZoomInfo?
answers.a: The contract is the most-cited frustration: annual lock-in with a strict 60–90 day cancellation window and 10–20% renewal increases. Credits burn fast, data can be stale (prospects who left years ago), and it's built for enterprise — overkill and overpriced for SMBs, with weaker accuracy outside the US.

accessiBe is genuinely best for small and medium sites on ordinary CMS templates whose owners want a visible, cheap first step — contrast, text sizing, keyboard hints and an accessibility statement — and who understand they are buying an aid rather than conformance. The visit-based tiers are honest for that use: at 5,000 visits a month $490 a year is real money but not a project budget, and the Scale tier is the only one that includes any human testing at all. Skip it if you need actual WCAG conformance, are responding to a demand letter, or run a complex web app with custom components — in all three the money belongs in an audit and code fixes, and an overlay will not stand in for either. Skip it too if you are shopping on the promise of automatic compliance. That promise is what the FTC ordered the company to stop making without evidence, so treat any version of it you still see as a reason to look harder, not to buy.

(2026-09-10, read on their own pricing page) Four tiers for accessWidget, priced per monthly website visits, with both a monthly and a yearly rate on every tier: Micro $59/month or $490/year up to 5,000 visits a month, Growth $179/month or $1,490/year up to 30,000, Scale $479/month or $3,990/year up to 100,000, and Enterprise on quote above that. Micro covers automated scans and fixes every 24 hours, an accessibility statement and report, and email plus live chat. Growth adds a dedicated case manager, Google Analytics integration, multi-account and team management, and a two-day response target. Scale adds one hour with an ADA attorney, a yearly round of manual testing and validation by their experts, and custom fixes. Enterprise adds 5 to 10 attorney hours, on-demand testing, SSO and a dedicated account manager. The page opens on the yearly toggle, so $490 is the first figure a visitor sees; switching it to 'Billed monthly' shows the monthly rates above. Paying yearly saves about 30% against twelve monthly payments, which is what the toggle's own SAVE 30% label claims. No free plan and no trial is listed. Always verify the live price.

answers.q: What is the catch with accessiBe?
answers.a:
The thing you most need to know about this product is not on its pricing page, it is on the FTC’s. In January 2025 the Federal Trade Commission ordered accessiBe to pay $1 million to settle allegations that it misrepresented what accessWidget does; the Commission approved the order as final in April 2025. The FTC’s position was that accessiBe’s claim that its AI plug-in could make any website conform to WCAG was false, misleading or unsubstantiated — the widget did not make all customer sites WCAG-compliant. The order now bars the company from claiming its automated products make a site WCAG-compliant, or keep it compliant over time, unless it holds evidence to back that up. It also requires disclosing the domain limitations of those products before you incur a financial obligation.

There is a second finding that belongs on a page like this one. The FTC also alleged accessiBe formatted third-party articles and reviews so they read as independent opinion while failing to disclose the company’s material connections to those reviewers; the order requires it to disclose such connections from here on. We are an affiliate of accessiBe and we get paid if you sign up through our link — which is exactly the sort of connection that case was about, and exactly why it is stated here rather than in a footnote.

What that means in practice: price this as a partial aid, not as legal cover. An overlay sits on top of a site and adjusts it in the browser. It cannot rewrite bad markup, fix an inaccessible custom component or make a keyboard trap go away, and no vendor’s automated layer can promise the conformance a real audit and remediation deliver. If you are buying to reduce the chance of a demand letter, buy the audit — the widget is not that. And the structural point behind the FTC order: accessWidget adjusts the page in the browser at load time rather than fixing the underlying markup, so the remediation exists only while the widget is being served. Stop paying and the site is exactly as accessible as it was before you started — which is the difference between renting a compliance layer and fixing a site.

doola is genuinely best for founders (often non-US) who want US LLC/C-Corp formation, EIN and compliance handled in one place without the paperwork. Skip it if you're a US resident comfortable filing formation yourself — the state fee plus a cheap registered agent costs far less than the bundle.

(re-verified 1 September 2026 on doola.com/pricing) The August sale has ended, so these are the list prices again. Starter is $297 a year plus state fees and covers LLC or C-Corp formation, EIN, a registered agent and a US address; state filing fees run $50 to $500 depending on the state, and they are yours, not doola's. Pulse bookkeeping comes with a 30-day trial and renews at $300 a year. Tax and Compliance, the tier the page marks Most Popular, is $1,999 a year plus state fees. Business-in-a-Box is $2,999 a year, or $329 a month, plus state fees. doola's own FAQ states that all plans are billed annually. Worth knowing for timing: through 31 August the page ran an automatic discount of up to $750 that could not be combined with anything else, which showed $222, $1,499 and $2,249 for those three tiers. That window closed on 31 August, which is precisely why our reader code applies again from 1 September. Always verify the live price.

answers.q: What is the catch with doola?
answers.a: Formation is the cheap part; the recurring bookkeeping and tax tiers are where the real cost sits, and state fees are extra on top of doola's price. Convenient especially for non-US founders, but a local accountant may be cheaper once you're established.

eDesk is genuinely best for e-commerce and marketplace sellers who want one unified inbox across Amazon, eBay, Shopify and email — with order data and AI-assisted replies where support and revenue overlap. Skip it if you run a non-commerce SaaS or service business (general helpdesks fit better and cheaper), or your ticket volume is low enough that a shared inbox already copes.

(re-verified 2026-08-17) Free plan to start; Essential $39 per agent/mo, Growth $89 (recommended), Professional $119, Enterprise custom — all billed annually, with monthly billing 20% higher ($49 against $39 on Essential). The AI Agent is included on every paid tier, but its automated resolutions bill separately at $0.99 per outcome: you pay when it actually resolves a query, not per attempt. eDesk claims the agent can automate up to 65% of support across channels, so model the outcome fee against your ticket volume — at 1,000 resolved tickets a month that is $990 on top of the seats. Always verify the live price.

answers.q: What is the catch with eDesk?
answers.a: There are two meters, and the second one is easy to miss. The per-agent price is the entry ticket, but the AI Agent charges $0.99 for every automated resolution on top. That is great when it deflects real tickets, but it is a variable line item that scales with your support volume — model it against your ticket count before assuming a flat bill. And the honest fundamental for any e-commerce helpdesk: the value is only as good as your marketplace integrations actually syncing — test Amazon/eBay/Shopify connections with your real accounts during the free trial.

folk is genuinely best for small sales teams, agencies and VC/partnership teams who want a clean, fast-to-set-up CRM with a great LinkedIn enrichment extension. Skip it if you need real multi-step workflow automation and reporting, or you are on Standard and want Zapier, Make or the REST API — folk keeps those for Premium and up, and is lightweight by design.

$30/member/month on Standard, $60 on Premium and from $100 on Enterprise when billed monthly; billed yearly those drop to $24, $48 and from $80 per member per month — 20% off — for $288, $576 and $960 per member per year (re-verified 2026-09-03; every figure held). The same page publishes euro rates: 27€, 54€ and from 83€ monthly, 22€, 43€ and from 67€ yearly, for 259€, 518€ and 804€ a year. The free trial is two weeks and needs no credit card; folk's own FAQ says an account that does not upgrade is blocked rather than deleted at the end, and that the trial can be extended by a week on request. The published caps: email enrichment 500 a month on Standard, 1,000 on Premium and custom on Enterprise; AI magic fields 2,000 and 5,000; account sync one per member and five per member. Always verify the live price.

answers.q: What is the catch with folk?
answers.a: One gap has closed and one has narrowed. folk now has a mobile app — the pricing table carries a Mobile app row ticked on all three plans — so the browser-only complaint is out of date. Automation is still uneven, but the picture moved in September: Zapier and Make stay Premium and Enterprise only, and so does the REST API, yet the table now carries an MCP row ticked on all three plans. Standard therefore does have a programmatic route — through an AI client rather than a workflow builder — and no plan shows a native multi-step workflow. Enrichment is capped at 500 a month on Standard and 1,000 on Premium, and email sequences need at least Premium.

iContact is genuinely best for small businesses and nonprofits who want a simple, reliable email tool with strong deliverability and a real marketing advisor included on every paid plan. Skip it if you need advanced multi-branch automation (ActiveCampaign does more) or you're chasing the rock-bottom cheapest option.

(re-verified 2026-08-17) No permanent free plan — a 30-day free trial, then paid tiers by contact count, with 15% off for paying yearly. At 500 contacts Standard is $9/mo and Premium $16/mo; the ladder then climbs with list size, with Standard running $14, $28, $45, $73, $110, $180, $250 and $350 a month at successive contact bands and Premium starting from $16 and $27 at the equivalent steps. Standard covers templates, landing pages and automations; Premium adds unlimited users, social posting and the AI content assistant. Larger lists are quoted. Always verify the live price.

answers.q: What is the catch with iContact?
answers.a: Pricing feels a touch high for what you get, and the Standard plan's hard caps on automations and landing pages push growing teams to upgrade sooner than expected. Set against ActiveCampaign the automation builder is the thinner half of the deal; what iContact sells instead is a product you can hold in your head, deliverability that holds up, and a human on support included rather than sold as a tier.

involve.me is genuinely best for marketers building interactive lead-gen — quizzes, calculators, assessments and payment funnels with built-in email sequences — who want a free tier to validate the concept first. Skip it if you just need a simple form (lighter tools do that free), or you don’t yet have the traffic to feed an interactive funnel.

(re-verified 19 September 2026 on the public pricing page; the free plan's feature set was measured inside the product, because the plan cards still do not state it) There is a free plan, and this is what it actually gives: 2 live funnels, publishing on a daanV.involve.me subdomain (or one of ten alternatives such as quizzes.cx, forms.ac and calculators.cx), the AI funnel builder, and involve.me branding on every page. No team seats at all. The pricing FAQ does publish the number that decides when it runs out: a free account runs to 50 submissions or 500 visits a month, and if you reach that without upgrading your funnels lock until the next calendar month starts. Paid, per person per month, annual against monthly: Start $29 / $49 with 3 live funnels and 1 user, Grow $69 / $99 with 5 funnels and 2 users, Scale $139 / $199 with 25 funnels, 5 users, A/B testing and lead verification. Enterprise is from $499/mo on annual contracts only. In the app the same tiers are priced in euros — €29, €69, €139 — and the annual toggle says “save up to 41%” where the public page says 40%. Two meters that decide more than the funnel count does are still missing from the tier pages: funnel visits a month (10,000 / 25,000 / 100,000) and contacts collected a month (300 / 1,000 / 3,000); the AI-credit allowance (50 / 100 / 300) is on the public comparison table. Each is toppable: +5,000 visits €8.33, +200 contacts €8.33, +250 AI credits €7.50, +1 seat €7.50, +5 live funnels €7.50. Prices exclude EU VAT. Every tier is higher than at the 17 Jul 2026 reading, when Start was $19/mo annual and $29 month-to-month. Always verify the live price.

answers.q: What is the catch with involve.me?
answers.a: The tier pages sell live funnels, but the meter that empties first is contacts. Start collects 300 contacts a month against 10,000 funnel visits — so a funnel converting at 3% hits the contact ceiling and the visit ceiling in the same week, and the next 200 contacts cost €8.33 on top. Those two meters appear only in the in-app comparison table; the public table publishes the AI-credit allowance but not visits or contacts. The free plan is documented in exactly one place, and not where you would look for it: the pricing FAQ caps it at 50 submissions or 500 visits a month and warns that your funnels lock until the next calendar month if you hit that without upgrading, while the plan cards say nothing at all about what it includes. We measured that part — 2 live funnels, involve.me branding, no team seats — and you only learn it by hitting the wall, because a free account has no usage panel: “Plans & Billing” goes straight to the upgrade page. And the honest fundamental for any interactive-funnel tool: quizzes and calculators convert traffic you already have — they don't create it, so validate on the free plan before the subscription outruns the pipeline.

lemlist is genuinely best for outbound teams that live in cold email and want multichannel sequences, warm-up and a big template community in one per-seat tool. Skip it if you send occasional one-off campaigns — the entry plan starts at 69€/month and only pays off with steady outbound volume.

(re-verified 2026-08-17; the page served us DOLLARS today where our previous reading was in euros, with the same numerals — check your own checkout) No free plan, 14-day trial. Email is $69/month, or $55/month on yearly billing, covering unlimited users and 50,000 emails a month. Multichannel is $109/month per user, or $87/month yearly, with unlimited emails and messages and 5 senders per user. Quarterly billing saves 10% and yearly 20%. Enterprise (5+ users) is quote-only. Contact data is billed separately through rechargeable credits where 1 credit = $0.01: a 1,000-credit pack is $10 and buys roughly 200 email lookups or 50 phone numbers, with a phone number costing 20 credits. Always verify the live price.

answers.q: What is the catch with lemlist?
answers.a: The per-seat plus per-email-account model makes total cost unpredictable as you scale, and reviews flag support response times and the LinkedIn Chrome-extension's reliability.

monday.com is genuinely best for teams who want one visual system for projects and work, and who will actually use the automations and views that justify the per-seat price at Standard or above. Skip it if you are two or three people who need a shared list. The free tier caps at 2 seats and 3 boards, and paying per seat for views you will not use is the most common way this gets expensive. Also skip it if you only want the CRM, since that is a separate subscription and worth pricing against dedicated CRMs.

(read 2026-08-26 on monday.com/pricing over a US connection, at their default of 10 seats on yearly billing) Free covers two seats. Basic is $9 per seat a month, a total of $90; Standard $12, down from $14, for $120 instead of $140; Pro $19, down from $22, for $190 instead of $220. Enterprise is quoted. The seat count is the thing to watch: the per-seat figure moves with team size, so a price read at ten seats is not what three or fifty will cost. Yearly billing is marked as 18% off, and each paid tier carries its own monthly AI-credit allowance rather than selling AI separately. Always verify the live price.

answers.q: What is the catch with monday.com?
answers.a: The seat price is not the product price. monday sells four products — Work Management, CRM, Dev and Service — each on its own subscription, and the $9 you see first is the cheapest tier of one of them. A sales team that wants the CRM is buying a second subscription on top of whatever Work Management costs, with a three-seat minimum of its own. The second number to find before you commit is the automation cap. Standard allows 250 automation actions a month across the whole account. If you are buying monday because of the automations you saw demoed, 250 is roughly one workflow running a few times a day — and the next step up is Pro at $19 a seat against Standard's $12. Free is capped at two seats and three boards, which makes it a preview rather than a plan.

noCRM is genuinely best for solo sellers, small outbound teams and telesales operations that want a list of leads each carrying a next step, rather than a CRM to configure — and European buyers who care that it is built and hosted in the EU, ISO 27001 certified and billed in euros. Skip it if you want email to live inside the tool without paying for the top tier, because Starter and Expert are BCC-only; you need WhatsApp, VoIP dialling or call recording, all of which are Dream-only; you are running a team and expected roles, permissions and performance reports below €33 a user a month; or you wanted a free plan rather than a 15-day trial.

(read 9 September 2026 on www.nocrm.io/pricing, in both billing modes) Three per-seat tiers and no free plan. The page opens on annual billing, where Starter is €11, Expert €22 and Dream €33 per user a month; switch the toggle to monthly and the same tiers are €19, €29 and €39. That makes the annual saving 42% on Starter, 24% on Expert and 15% on Dream, so the "save up to 40%" badge is carried entirely by the cheapest tier. Starter is capped at 500 leads in a single pipeline with at most four custom fields, and it is sold to new customers only. Every tier includes 5,000 emails a month and all users on one account must sit on the same plan. There is no free tier: a 15-day trial runs without a credit card, or 30 days if you add one, and the account is paused rather than downgraded when it ends. Checkout is through Stripe, and 20% VAT is added for French companies and for EU businesses without a valid VAT number.
