One thing to read twice — in the annual view the Starter card reads €11/user/year while the comparison table directly beneath it reads €11/user/month for the same plan. The month is the correct one: it is what the page's own plan data carries for every other tier and what the monthly figure of €19 is measured against. Always verify the live price.

answers.q: What is the catch with noCRM?
answers.a: The pitch is that salespeople hate CRMs, and the answer is a tool built around the next action rather than the form. What the plan table shows is that almost everything a sales team needs to work that way sits on the top tier. Two-way email sync is Dream at €33 a user; on Starter and on Expert, email is BCC only, which means you copy noCRM on outgoing mail and read replies elsewhere. WhatsApp lead creation and conversation sync are Dream. The VoIP integrations the homepage leads with — CloudTalk, JustCall, Aircall, power dialling, call recording, transcripts — are Dream. Roles and permissions, lead assignment, team goal tracking and team performance reports are Dream. Internal automations are Dream. noCRM's own FAQ calls Expert "the best fit for most teams", and Expert has no team management in it at all. So the honest way to read the ladder is that Starter and Expert are versions for one person — a lead list with follow-ups, and then the same thing without the caps — while the product the marketing describes starts at €33 a user a month on annual billing, or €39 monthly. That is three times the entry price, and it is the number to budget from if more than one person is selling. Two smaller things. Starter is restricted to new customers, so it is not a tier you can fall back to when a year on Expert turns out to be more than you needed. And there is no free plan behind the trial: 15 days, or 30 if you hand over a card first.

rePete is genuinely best for Shopify stores selling consumables or anything with a natural replenishment rhythm — coffee, supplements, pet food, skincare — whose customers refuse subscriptions but do come back, and who would rather pay for results than carry another monthly app fee. Skip it if your repeat revenue is already large, because an uncapped 3% overtakes any subscription app well before six figures; your customers buy once and rarely return, where there is no reorder moment to predict; or you cannot get comfortable with an app that can edit orders, discounts and the storefront.

(read 19 September 2026 in a live browser on repete.me/pricing and on the App Store listing at apps.shopify.com/reorder-service) There is no subscription and no tier. rePete is free to install and takes a percentage of the sales it claims to have caused, billed in USD, on three rates that are defined by a clock rather than by judgement.

Direct Sales is 3%, charged when rePete nudges a customer to reorder a product and they complete the purchase within 24 hours. Assisted Sales is 1%, charged on the same nudge when the purchase lands within 7 days. Upsells and cross-sells are 5%, charged on any extra items the customer adds beyond the reorder product itself.

What the page rules out is as useful as what it charges: no SMS fees, no email fees, no per-contact fees, no push fees, no app fees and no minimums. So the messaging channels — email, SMS, WhatsApp and on-site — carry no cost of their own, which is unusual in a category where SMS is normally metered separately. There is no published ceiling, no volume discount and no negotiated rate: the percentages are the whole price list. The app is built by Bold of Winnipeg, Shopify's first front-end app developer and the team behind Bold Subscriptions; it launched on 4 July 2025 and holds 5.0 from nine reviews. Always verify the live price.

answers.q: What is the catch with rePete?
answers.a:
The pricing is honest and the arithmetic still deserves care, because this is a percentage with no ceiling on it. There is no cap, no volume discount and no tier: 3% of attributed reorders at $5,000 a month is $150, at $50,000 it is $1,500, and at $200,000 it is $6,000 — for the same software. Most Shopify apps stop charging more once you pass their top tier; this one never does. If rePete works, the bill grows exactly as fast as the result, which is the deal you are signing rather than a trap, but it is the opposite shape to every subscription app you are comparing it against.

The seven-day window is where I would push back. Direct Sales at 3% requires the purchase within 24 hours of the nudge, which is a strong causal claim. Assisted Sales at 1% counts anything that lands within seven days — and a customer who buys coffee, supplements or pet food every month was going to reorder in that window anyway. You will pay 1% on a quantity of revenue that would have arrived without the message, and there is no way to tell from the outside how much. Ask for the split between direct and assisted in your first month before you judge the return.

The highest rate sits on the smallest claim. Upsells and cross-sells are 5%, charged on any extra item added beyond the reorder product — so a customer who reorders and adds one more thing pays 3% on the first and 5% on the second. That is the most expensive rate on the page attached to the action rePete has the weakest claim to have caused.

The evidence base is thin rather than bad. Nine reviews, all five-star, the visible ones from early September 2026 and describing two to three months of use. That is real usage by named stores, and it is still nine.

One thing to read before installing: the data scope is wide. The listing asks to view sensitive customer data, and to view *and edit* customers, products, orders, discounts, shop analytics and the online store. That is consistent with an app that writes discounts and builds carts, but it is a lot of reach for a tool you are trying on a commission basis.

respond.io is genuinely best for a small team that already lives in WhatsApp and Instagram DMs and has outgrown a shared phone — retail, clinics, travel, local services. Per-contact pricing suits you if headcount grows faster than conversation volume, and the seven-day trial without a card lets you check that before committing. Skip it if you only need one channel: a plain shared inbox or a helpdesk will cost less than an omnichannel platform you use a fifth of. Skip the Starter plan specifically if automation is the reason you are looking — you will be on Growth within a month. And if your monthly active contacts run into the tens of thousands, get the number in writing first, because that is the meter and the published ladder stops being informative.

(2026-08-13, read off respond.io/pricing) Four tiers, billed on monthly active contacts rather than seats: Starter $79/month, Growth $159, Advanced $279, and Enterprise on quote. Paying yearly takes roughly 20% off — $948, $1,908 and $3,348 a year against $1,188, $2,388 and $4,188 monthly. The trial is 7 days and takes no card. What separates the tiers is not volume but capability, and the line matters: Starter buys team and custom inboxes, the mobile app, AI Prompt, AI Assist, basic reports and 2FA. **Workflows automation, broadcasts, AI Agents, advanced reports, the developer API and the Zapier and Make integrations all start at Growth.** Advanced adds multiple workspaces, SSO, webhooks, HTTP requests in workflows and phone-number masking, and although a figure is shown its button says “Talk to Sales”. One thing we could not pin down. The page carries a selector for 1,000 / 2,500 / 5,000 / 10,000 / more than 10,000 monthly active contacts under the heading “pay only for the contacts you talk to”, but the prices we read did not move between those settings. Ask what your contact volume actually costs before you sign — that is the meter you are buying. Always verify the live price.

answers.q: What is the catch with respond.io?
answers.a: The entry plan is the inbox without the engine. At $79 you get shared inboxes across WhatsApp, Instagram, Messenger, SMS and live chat, and that alone solves the “five people answering from one phone” problem. But workflow automation, broadcasts, AI Agents and the API — the things most people picture when they read “omnichannel platform” — begin at $159, so the real entry price for an automated setup is double the headline. Work out which side of that line you sit on before comparing it with anything else. And note the meter: you pay per active contact per month, so cost follows how many people message you, not how many staff you add. That is kinder than per-seat pricing for a small team fielding a lot of chats, and harsher if you have a big list you talk to often.
